Overview
Nobody really knows what happened. Somewhere in the remote expanses of Turkmenistan there is a crater that has been flaming since at least 1971. The combination of Soviet record-keeping and Soviet engineering means that we can only speculate as to why this wonder of the Soviet world exists. Perhaps they were drilling for natural gas and caused a collapse, then opted to light the ensuing crater to prevent the spread of toxic gases. Perhaps someone got drunk and flicked a cigarette in the thing, because Soviets.
In any case, once you fly into the Turkmen capital you can reach the thing in four hours. The road is not marked; the only accommodations are some crude yurts around the crater. Still, if you have the patience to acquire a visa and the bull-headedness to wander out into the wilderness you, too, can walk towards nothing in particular until you are suddenly there, at the Door To Hell.
In the native tongue they call it Ohio State University.
[AFTER THE JUMP: not your usual Door To Hell]

Run Offense vs OSU

Marshall likely a non factor unfortunately [Fuller]
OSU's defense has taken a significant step back this year. Last year they were about the best defense in the country, second in adjusted EPA/play allowed behind Texas Tech and first in SP+. This year they've dipped to 23rd and 15th in those stats.
This is in part because they lost an ungodly amount of talent to the NFL, but there are also chinks in the armor that have started revealing themselves now that second-year defensive coordinator Matt Patricia has looked down after his Wile E Coyote year. Eleven Warriors contributor Ross Fulton, who I've never known to be anything but level-headed, was almost wroth after OSU gave up 31 to Nebraska in a loss. Ironically, the stuff that OSU struggled the most against was a variety of College Crappe that is Jason Beck's wheelhouse:
OSU never had the numbers/was consistently out leveraged against bluff read. https://t.co/f2QZqcqejr
— Ross Fulton (@RossRFulton) November 22, 2026

I'd imagine OSU has looked at the film and will not be so vulnerable on Saturday, but Patricia is a dyed-in-the-wool NFL guy and—as we saw with Wink Martindale—those dudes can have enormous blind spots. On top of being an NFL guy, Patricia was a decidedly unsuccessful NFL guy as soon as he left Bill Belichick's side; it's possible Michigan might be able to scheme up some easy wins.
I think that if Bryant Haines was the OSU DC with the same group of players OSU would be 10-1 right now.
— Ross Fulton (@RossRFulton) November 22, 2026

Alas: I'd feel better about this possibility if Michigan had an offensive coordinator.
Still, Michigan did do some things right against UCLA and Savion Hiter finally looked like someone who could have been a highly touted recruit. With Underwood expected to start, a heavy dose of zone read stuff may find Michigan exploring the space in ways you might not expect.
I still expect a bunch of errors that put Michigan behind the chains and not a whole lot of consistency.
KEY MATCHUP: HITER/UNDERWOOD vs EXPLOSIVES. If given an opportunity both guys can finish a long run.
Pass Offense vs OSU

ok please do it again [Barron]
This phase has been downright mediocre. OSU is 54th in EPA/dropback allowed and the trend here has been strongly negative. OSU has not held an opponent under seven yards an attempt since battering the corpse of Maryland six games ago. Only USC has really cracked them for impressive numbers (9.7 YPA) but opponents have consistently ripped off chunks without much in the way of response; OSU has just two interceptions against non-MAC opponents this year, one of them a ridiculous fluke.
PFF is relatively sanguine about their coverage, with few negative outliers amongst the most deployed Buckeyes. CB2 Devin Sanchez is thoroughly mediocre and can get shook; a couple of OSU LBs are also in the yellow-to-red zone. Alex on the OSU secondary:
Seeing the kind of passing success that Nebraska was having made me a little more pessimistic, in that I don't think Michigan, as it stands, has the QB play (or possibly receiver ammo) to replicate that. There weren't many coverage busts and I don't think that Mathews nor Devin Sanchez are bad. The Nk Jay Timmons has also become an important part of this defense, an excellent cover guy out of the slot as a freshman. And obviously I'm a fan of Little over the top + Jaylen McClain.

Where OSU struggles is pass rush. Edge Kenyatta Jackson is a solid option but not a game-wrecker; his 12% win rate is C+ level. OSU also gets the occasional pressure from their starting DTs; everyone else is a non-factor save for a couple of rotational guys who are Jackson-ish. Incredibly, this adds up to the #102 graded pass rush in the country, per PFF. I'd say something about how the mighty have fallen but then I remember JTT's career 9% win rate.
How much this weakness helps Michigan is an open question. Blake Frazier, previously thought to have shut it down for the season, is questionable on this week's injury report. Insider chatter seems to believe he will play, which will be a massive upgrade on a game but nowhere near ready Marky Walbridge. A dinged Frazier can probably hold off OSU ends with a consistency Walbridge won't.
If Underwood is unmolested in the pocket we've seen him do some work, particularly against Iowa. His problem is the Michigan WR corps, which will not have JJ Buchanan and may or may not have Andrew Marsh. Marsh did not play last week after being questionable in the middle of the week and has that indecent exposure charge that Michigan seems to be ignoring. Having Marsh is critical… but also may be detrimental because when Marsh is in and Buchanan is not Underwood throws to Marsh no matter what is happening.
So: despite the seeming permeability of this unit, Michigan seems spectacularly ill-equipped to take advantage of it. When OSU blitzes, which they do a lot, will Michigan pick it up? Eh… maybe. If they don't, will Underwood find a hot route? Probably not. Will the receivers separate from okay to good OSU corners? Marsh, if he plays, can, but if OSU just goes with a Jeremiah Smith gameplan on him I have trouble seeing Underwood rely on Michigan's other options.
Survey says it doesn't really matter what the opposition D looks like. This passing game is broken.
KEY MATCHUP: MASON BONNER vs LET IT RIDE. When you suck a 6'7" leapy guy against a potentially injured nickel seems like a good option.
Run Defense vs OSU

not that Bo Jackson [Bryan Fuller]
Ryan Day will occasionally grow a mustache under his beard and declare that the Ohio State Buckeyes are tough and will manball you; then he forgets about it and his team dips into triple digits in short yardage conversions. OSU looks to be about midway through this cycle, sporting a ground game that is superficially decent but looks like the kind that Michigan can keep in check. The following chart is raw EPA/rush for OSU's season:

The three positive outliers are against Illinois (94th in rush EPA D) the week they fired their defensive coordinator, the smoking husk of Maryland (98th), and Lincoln Riley (117th). Indiana, Iowa, Texas, and… uh… Kent State all put OSU in negative EPA/rush. Michigan has a pretty good shot at replicating that; they're 5th in EPA/rush allowed. Iowa is 1st, Texas 12th, Indiana 34th. Variance happens; OSU and Michigan's seasons suggest that this should be a slog for the Buckeyes.
Bo Jackson (Not That Bo Jackson) is the starter and has gotten about two-thirds of OSU running back carries. Second stringer Ja'Kobi Jackson went out with a foot injury a few weeks ago and will not play, leaving Isaiah West as the backup. Survey says this is going to be 90% Jackson since West has fumbled three times in the last four games and OSU has no playoff aspirations to bother with. Despite being a moxie scramble guy, QB Luke Fahey has barely been used in designed runs. That may change in this game; as it stands I would expect to to be almost all Jackson.
Unfortunately, Michigan has not choked out opposition ground games the Minter/Macdonald way by having superstar defensive tackles who can be left alone. Michigan brings a lot of heat and the DTs can suffer blowouts if doubled. I might say "okay" to that if it meant perpetual Jeremiah Smith bracket but there is a level of damage the OSU ground came can do that would make that approach untenable.
OSU may in fact be able to do this since the biggest problem with their ground game is a lack of explosive plays. Without a running QB or an intricate Harbaugh-esque run scheme explosives generally come down to your back making something happen, and while Jackson has a number of assets he is not hugely explosive or jittery. They've been good at acquiring line yards and avoiding stuffed plays; there's enough there that an even numbers box could go either way. I expect Hill to try some Minter Lite in this game's early phases to see if he can get away with it; I don't expect him to get away with it.
KEY MATCHUP: MICHIGAN DTs vs THE GHOSTS OF 13-10. Boy howdy could this team use an outlier performance from a couple DTs. This would really force a freshman QB to throw into the teeth of a defense.
Pass Defense vs OSU

go away please [Barron]
When Julian Sayin got knocked out for the year it wasn't ultra-hyped sophomore Tavien St Clair who came in but rather three-star freshman Luke Fahey. Fahey is one of those moxie gamer types with a lot of escapability,—his sack-to-pressure ratio is 60% of Sayin's—but without the NFL stature a guy like Sayin has. OSU lists him at 5'11", and if you're listed at 5'11" you're not 5'11".
Fahey's been surprisingly good for a guy thrown into the fire. He's a couple YPA short of Sayin's numbers but hasn't put the ball into danger much and has kept hurling it in the general direction of the best player in college football. Is he good? I don't know. Does he have to be? Not really.
That's because of the aforementioned. Ohio State is massively dependent on Jeremiah Smith, who likely needs no introduction to Michigan fans. He needs no introduction to anyone who's heard of football, probably. Smith has a whopping 122 targets this season, of which he's caught an equally whopping 86 balls for an even more whopping 1482 yards. That's 17 yards a catch, which is unsurprising since his average depth of target is almost 15 yards. He's 22 of 38 on contested opportunities this season, which is another stat that could be labeled "whopping." He's likely to win the Heisman on a team that will finish, at best, 8-4. There's not a whole lot else you have to say.
Fortunately for Michigan, and the rest of the world, it looks like the never-ending MechaHitler wide receiver assembly line OSU has had for a decade may be drying up. OSU's second leading receiver is UTSA transfer Devin McCuin, who is fine. He's got 32 catches for 406 yards and PFF regards him as just a guy.
Past McCuin there's very little. Presumed #2 Brandon Inniss has not played since the Indiana game in week seven despite supposedly being cleared two weeks ago; even before that he was close to a non-entity with a total of 39 yards in four games against non-MAC opponents. 6'5" freshman Chris Henry has 11 catches on the season; these are bombs (26 yards a catch) but two drops on sixteen targets is a negative indicator. No other wideout has made an impact. Instead OSU has used Jackson plus TEs Nate Roberts and Mason Williams as checkdown/outlet options when Smith is triple covered.
OSU pass protection has been sort of iffy. PFF has them 44th; right tackle has been an issue. The individual grades outside of that spot are all good but not great; this could be an opportunity for Dom Nichols to write his name in rivalry history. Or perhaps John Henry Daley.
I expect Smith to get the mother of all brackets until OSU proves that Michigan can no longer do this; chances are they'll not suffer enough to get off of it. Michigan's defensive backs are good enough to put out there against your UTSA transfers and cope. Meanwhile, Fahey to Not Smith is very beatable:

SPECIAL TEAMS
This has also not been a strength. Despite going 12/14 on the season, kicker Connor Hawkins is almost perfectly mediocre at 63rd in FG efficiency; punter Joe McGuire and OSU coverage teams see OSU 99th in punt efficiency; OSU is also 106th in kickoff efficiency. Punt coverage has been a problem of late, with a 44-yarder ceded to USC, 3 returns for 51 yards by Northwestern, and a 21-yarder given up to Nebraska in the last four weeks.

michigan.headline: Michigan Mailbag: Will Michigan or Ohio State hire a new head coach after The Game?
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 21: Head Coach Kyle Whittingham of the Michigan Wolverines looks on during the third quarter against the UCLA Bruins at Michigan Stadium on November 21, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

It’s hard to believe we’re about to watch the Michigan Wolverines play their last game of the 2026 regular season. What was mostly a slog still had some bright spots. At the end of the day, I’m writing this, and you’re reading it because we love the sport of college football.

It’s tough to believe that this year’s edition of The Game might be one of the least hyped yet. It’s a storied rivalry, but the preseason expectations were much higher for these programs than what transpired.

For Ohio State, losing QB Julian Sayin to injury really hurt the offense, and without a roster to straight-up out-talent everyone, the defense isn’t nearly as daunting. Still, it’s clear Ohio State has the edge. The game is in Columbus.

We asked you to post your questions on The Feed ahead of the game:

How can Michigan stop WR Jeremiah Smith?

It’s no secret that WR Jeremiah Smith has a ton of talent. He’s one of the favorites to win the Heisman Trophy this year, because he’s just that good. He’s managed 1,482 yards already this season, with 17 touchdowns to boot. Only a few teams have managed to hold him to under 100 yards, and a few of those Ohio State had such a significant lead that Smith didn’t play the entire game.

Michigan’s defense, believe it or not, will still be one of the toughest defenses Ohio State has played this season. The only defense the Buckeyes have played that ranks higher than Michigan is Nebraska. I’m sure you’re aware at this point, but Nebraska beat the Buckeyes last Saturday. Michigan has talented cornerbacks, like Jyaire Hill and Zeke Berry, who know what this rivalry means. They have the chance to live up to the moment and make some big plays. I’m also hoping that Fahey isn’t as familiar with S Rod Moore, who I can see trying to make a big play in this one, too.

I sort of laid this out above, but I agree, keeping Smith under 100 yards would certainly be nice. It’s tough to say he won’t get into the end zone; Michigan’s defense has had miscues in every single game this season.

I’d expect Ohio State to capitalize on a drive or two. Michigan can’t afford to play like they did on the road at Oregon if they want a chance to win this one. I think the game plan needs to involve relying on its defensive line to force QB Luke Fahey to throw under pressure.

In a game this big, it’s tough not to see Fahey forcing something to Smith that might go the other way. It’s impossible to stop Smith completely, but it’s possible to rattle a quarterback with a lot of pressure on him in the biggest rivalry in sports.

What’s next for each program?

At the time I’m writing this, I have to say false. Which feels a little disappointing.

Michigan made headlines again this week when news surfaced that Trev Alberts would NOT become Michigan’s next AD. While the story feels more embarrassing than that, all you really need to know is that Michigan is once again searching for a new athletic director.

The path for the Wolverines to move on from Kyle Whittingham narrowed significantly after that announcement. Why would a lame-duck AD move on from a coach he fired to get the program in the right direction? Along with that, new President C. Cybele Raver looks to have gotten ahead of the Board of Regents.

This process clearly won’t be handled without everyone feeling like they were the reason for Michigan’s success in the future. I just don’t know that the higher-ups have their ducks in a row enough to move on from Whittingham in a way that will help the program next season. The new coach would be behind when it comes to the transfer portal and recruiting.

This is a mess.

As for Ryan Day, I think it’s a little more possible to see Ohio State moving on from him after a loss to Michigan, but the administration has backed him in the past. This season, it’s easy to blame the program’s failures this season on the injury to a starting quarterback.

That being said, his record isn’t great when he’s competing against other schools with top-tier talent. He also lost a longtime recruiter and coordinator, Brian Hartline, which will probably continue to hurt the program in the coming years.

So, I wouldn’t be surprised if Ryan Day gets fired; the fan base certainly feels some apathy toward this team, but I also wouldn’t be surprised if the administration still backs Day.

I said this a little in my last answer, but I’m just not sure there’s a realistic path to move on from Whittingham that doesn’t put this program even more behind than it already is.

The ineptitude of the university’s administration and board of regents has made it nearly impossible to move forward from a football coach. I don’t think there’s any way you can rush towards hiring a new football coach when you’ve decided to move on from your AD candidate because of something that could have been found easily by anyone using their own computer.

The only quick fix I see at this point is maybe naming Defensive Coordinator Jay Hill the interim while you work out the whole AD situation, but I don’t know if he’d do that.

Thanks for a great season, and some great questions. Let’s keep the conversation going. Post your thoughts in the comments below!

michigan.headline: Friday Discussion: Would a win over Ohio State save Kyle Whittingham’s job?
michigan.body:
No one will argue the 2026 Michigan football season has been anything other than an abject disaster. The Wolverines lost five games before mid-November, including rivalry games to Minnesota and Michigan State, and should have lost to Western Michigan if not for a miraculous Hail Mary.

The fan base has turned on first-year coach Kyle Whittingham. However, he and his staff achieved a slight reprieve last Saturday by upsetting UCLA. The season is still an unabashed failure, but it was very nice to send out the seniors (Rod Moore, specifically) with a huge home win.

As of this writing, it would still be more surprising than not if Whittingham has an office in Schembechler Hall next season. However, would a win in The Game change the calculus?

The Buckeyes are in the midst of their own apocalyptic season, having lost three of their last four games and four total, the most for them since 2011 when they went 6-7 overall. Discussions have started regarding the job security of head coach Ryan Day. There is virtually nothing to play for tomorrow for the players other than dignity and pride. However, that should be all you need in The Game. As for the coaches, everything could be on the line.

Should Michigan win, Whittingham would finish his first season at the helm with a 7-5 record with wins over Oklahoma, UCLA and Ohio State. He also has some ugly losses in Minnesota, Michigan State and Indiana, in the style they lost those ones.

If Whittingham were 30 years younger, there would no doubt be more lenience. However, he was never the long-term solution, has derailed the program and (likely) pushed a majority of the roster to the transfer portal. The complete and utter lack of player development is also alarming, as we’ve seen more than a few players visibly regress from 2025 to 2026. That shouldn’t happen in college football.

In case you can’t tell, I lean on the side of firing Whittingham regardless of the outcome of tomorrow’s game. Is there a case to be made for the flip side?

Whittingham was hired for a reason — he was a great coach who preached toughness and physicality throughout his career at Utah. He also hit a home run in his hire of Jay Hill as defensive coordinator. If Whittingham can hire an elite offensive coordinator and retain Hill, Michigan could be in business.

The offensive line was also ravaged with injuries this season. Jake Guarnera is the only starter who has played every game, and even he has been battling through an injury for a good chunk of the season. Michigan has also been without right tackle in Andrew Sprague since Week 2, while also seeing guys like Brady Norton, Nathan Efobi and Blake Frazier get banged up at various points this season, with Frazier still recovering from an injury he suffered a couple weeks back. A healthy offensive line in 2027 do work wonders on changing the narrative of the program.

Whittingham has also preached he never was afforded a full portal/recruiting cycle. While I have my doubts as to how much talent he could acquire, we can’t rule that out without seeing how that would play out. There’s a world Michigan is competitive again in 2027.

There are other nuances we have not even discussed, such as the hiring (or lack thereof) of an athletic director and which current Wolverines will enter the portal once it opens in January. Those things will certainly play a factor in the final decision.

With all that said, where do you land on the “Fire Whitt” spectrum? Should he be gone no matter what happens in The Game? If Michigan wins, would you be satisfied giving Whittingham another season? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

The thing about Mars: he's like a mediocre Cover 1 defense, in that you should defeat him no problem as long as you have some competence, but we're not sure Michigan does.

starts around 12:20pm

The Sayin injury has hurt them since Fahey is a limited freshman, but he has some moxie, and can execute an offense/throw the ball at Jeremiah Smith. Bo Jackson has picked it up with Ja'Kobi Jackson out. They returned last year's OL mostly but the Minnesota transfer RT is out and they're still mostly just guys (save for Sierveld). They use a lot more 2TE, which is Meta Game adjustment and also a reflection of Brandon Inniss being out and their WR room not having anyone after Jeremiah. Going to put more pressure on Moa.

Defensively Matt Patricia is starting to show his NFL GUY-ness after riding last year's talent wave to an elite defense. Still have some stars, including DT Eddrick Houston and SS Earl Little Jr. A lot of players are good—Devin Sanchez and Jermaine Matthews (who's questionable) are decent highly ranked CBs, Jaylen McClain is back from last year, and Bama transfer Qua Russaw is a little muck a muck. We will also ask them to tell us what's changed in the field of player compensation in the last few years, and lay out the field—how much big time universities are actually paying, where the money comes from, what's the difference between NIL, MMR, and House revenue, and how the rules are changing. 4. After Further Review: UCLA and Basketball's Bad Trip to Vegas

starts around 1:15pm

Brian didn't UFR the offense but we'll try to extract some takes on Underwood. I did UFR the defense and want to shout out some of the lads. Some of the guys who can stay are worth getting excited about. Jay Hill for interim HC?
Vegas: Blech. Brian was right: they're not a good team. Michigan ran into some terrible shot luck against Creighton and Miami, but they would have lost anyways. Boynton's offense looks broken, with the guards asked to do too much and the forwards unable to do anything but rebound occasionally.

Featured Musician: Oblivion

Yes roller derby fans: that's Kitty Kat second from left. [Lauren Colchamiro]
Tres Crow was a sophomore at Michigan, his band Ka-Tet had broken up, and his best friend/jam partner Seth (hi!) was studying abroad when his mom suggested he put up a flier. Two guitarists: Jason Evans and Ben Umanov, and a drummer Scott Lauffer answered. Tres met bassist Nathan Zamarron was met at a party. The band hit like lightning in Ann Arbor, for a time challenging Donkey Punch as the most surefire act to fill a Tuesday night at the Blind Pig. They had an incredible Battle of the Bands winning streak that was ended by one vote by Tally Hall. But they were hard to pin down. Lauffer was older, a double-bassing, odd-signatures metal-level technician. Tres was an intellectual pop writer. Jason was an experimental orchestral guitarist, while Ben was heavily influenced by Pink Floyd, and Nate by Tool. The mix was a technical, guitar-driven brand of rock music laden with heavy riffs and complex, ephemeral interludes and a TON of energy. This hit live, but didn't translate as well to their albums: the early "Ultrasound EP", 2001's "..." (often called "dot-dot-dot" or "ellipsis" or "self-titled"), and 2003's "The Garden in the Machine."
This wasn't a great time in general for an indie proggy sorta heavy too-smart meld of influences, and the band broke up in 2005, with Lauffer moving on and the rest of the band choosing not to go forward with a new, more focused album, a new drummer, a new New York label, and all of the national touring that would entail. Tres had some success in music with solo projects two bands Greenland and the Noble Three out of Nashville; he become a writer and businessman who builds sustainable green spaces in Atlanta. Ben founded Metalsucks (where he went by Vince Neilstein), sold that a few years ago, and manages a few bands while raising kids crops in upstate New York. Scott is still around Ann Arbor, and designs workplaces. Nate is the VP of LexArts, which manages community arts programs (basically the local NEA field office) in Lexington, KY. Jason is a nurse who saved thousands of lives during COVID; he lives in Ferndale, and will be watching The Game with me on Saturday. If you cannot tell, these are my best friends. I managed their merch during the band years, went on the road with them, and always intended to write a book about the band that Had It but never Made It.

michigan.headline: Michigan Hockey Preview: Wolverines look to sweep Ferris State before Wisconsin clash
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 13: Aidan Park #16 of the Michigan Wolverines celebrates with the Michigan bench following his second period goal against the Penn State Nittany Lions at Yost Ice Arena on November 13, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Michigan (11-2) won the fight and split the series with Michigan State and now turns its sights to lowly Ferris State (1-8-3) in the penultimate series before the winter break.

The Wolverines will fortunately be able to add forward Aidan Park (1G) and Henry Mews (6A) back to the lineup this week after one-game suspensions. And Mews might even be tasked with playing some forward this week, with three players — Nic Sima, Josh Nesbitt and Adam Valentini — serving the second of a two-game suspension on Friday night.

Albeit shorthanded, Michigan should still be able to build momentum as top-ranked Wisconsin awaits next weekend.

The Wolverines will heavily rely on their top stars to salt away the Bulldogs in Game 1. The newest future Detroit Red Wing — Michael Hage — still leads the country with 21 assists and 26 total points, and Jayden Perron still leads nationally with 14 goals and is second with 25 points. Moreover, of the 14 points awarded in the win over Michigan State, Michigan will have 12 accounted for on Friday despite playing shorthanded. Also, keep an eye on Cole McKinney (7G, 7A), who is quietly sixth nationally in faceoff wins and first in the Big Ten.

On the blue line, the Landon DuPont hype train is out of control and he hasn’t even scored a goal yet. DuPont’s 15 assists are third in the country and the presumptive top pick in next year’s NHL Draft is getting better every week. The D corps will need to assist where they can without three forwards, so in addition to Mewsy potentially moving to offense, head coach Brandon Naurato could move DuPont or Drew Schock (5G, 9A) up to a fourth-line role as well.

In net, the slump is over! Goaltender Jack Ivankovic was outstanding against Michigan State. Kovie posted a ridiculous .974 save percentage in Michigan’s win and a .943 in the handicapped shutout loss. With Kovie playing back to form, Ferris State is going to struggle to score regardless of who is playing in front of him. One goal of support might be all he needs to secure the win until reinforcements arrive on night two.

Ferris State

There is no way to sugarcoat this… Ferris State is a bad team. The Bulldogs — out of 63 teams — rank No. 61 in scoring offense and No. 56 in scoring defense. Ferris State’s lone win of the season did come in upset fashion over No. 12 Michigan Tech, but this team was thoroughly dominated in its other ranked series, losing by a combined score of 11-1 to Western Michigan.

Sophomore forward Justin Stupka leads this team with seven points on the season, a mark that would place him 10th on the Wolverines. A pair of Nathan’s round out the top three scorers with freshman Nathan Leek (2G, 4A) one point off the pace, and leading goal-scorer, junior Nathan Mackie (4G, 1A), one point away from Leek.

Defensively, senior Jack Mesic (4A) is the primary puck-mover, but freshman Urban Podrekar (3A) might be their most talented D-man. However, that only holds true if he can stay out of the penalty box. Podrekar has spent nine more minutes in the penalty box than the second most penalized Bulldog.

Freshman Alan Lendak has posted a .894 save percentage through 10 starts between the pipes and is responsible for securing Ferris State’s only win of the season. Junior Martin Lundberg has spelled Lendak twice this season, but his .839 save percentage surely cannot give the Bulldogs enough confidence to have him rotate against the Wolverines.

Key to the game

Don’t look ahead. Friday night could be the ultimate trap game of the season. Michigan is down a few players playing an inferior opponent one week before a collision with No. 1 Wisconsin. But as the Bulldogs showed against Tech, this team can pull the upset. The Wolverines need to take this series one game at a time and soundly put the Bulldogs away both nights before turning their attention to the Badgers. If Michigan can play myopic hockey against Ferris State, the Wolverines should have no problem securing multi-goal wins in each game.

michigan.headline: Michigan at No. 21 Ohio State Preview: Hot seat hot potato
michigan.body:
The narratives are endless, but completely foreign at the same time. The Michigan Wolverines are no longer playing for bowl eligibility, and they better not be playing to save Kyle Whittingham’s job; after the upset of UCLA last weekend, The Game is now all about pride — and the potential to cause some further humiliation, and stress, for their bitter rivals (and their leader).

For the Ohio State Buckeyes, this was supposed to be about backing into the College Football Playoff after a generous No. 14 ranking last weekend. Instead, a hilarious stumble at Nebraska made it four losses on the season, all but ending those CFP dreams. Now, Ryan Day is at risk of the unthinkable: a 7-5 record, matching Michigan’s, which would make him 1-5 since Covid in the Only Game That Matters.

So yea, there is a lot to play for, even if that is more on a local scale than a national one. Fans and players on both sides will not need to muster up extra motivation on Saturday, even if these are not the normal circumstances for this contest. Hate is not dependent on record or playoff odds, and the storylines are impossible to look away from when these beleaguered rivals fight to save face in Columbus.

Michigan (6-5, 3-5) at No. 21 Ohio State (7-4, 5-3)

Date & Time: Saturday, Nov. 28, noon ET
Location: Ohio Stadium, Columbus, OH
TV/Streaming: FOX

As nearly always is the case, Ohio State enters as the favorite. That did not stop the 2022 team from using its “five big plays” to win as underdogs, and the last trip to The Horseshoe saw an even more dramatic spread completely ignored as the Wolverines comically pulled off the historic upset. This game probably needs to replicate the style of that 2024 contest if Michigan wants to make it five of the last six in this rivalry (still a wild sentence to say).

Offense: Toughness

The way Michigan has owned Ohio State this decade is in the trenches. This year, the offense is just 116th in YPC with very few positive afternoons on the ground, making this recipe quite questionable. However, the passing game is even less viable, even with Andrew Marsh back, so the Wolverines will have no choice but to go back to the well that has been the source of victory so many times before.

Perhaps the biggest reason for optimism in this department is the Buckeye defense looking more like it did at the start of the decade than over the past couple seasons. Gone are a bunch of NFL-level defensive players and in their stead is a run defense that has allowed 13 touchdowns against Power Four opponents this season. Toughness is a cliche, but in every Ohio State loss it felt like teams could run at will against Matt Patricia’s group.

Savion Hiter is obviously the name to watch, and injury limitations to Jordan Marshall have seen the freshman get a chance to really embrace the primary role, hitting 100 yards in each of the last two weeks (against solid defenses). He should get plenty of opportunities on Saturday as the Wolverines try to set the tone. The run game has to include Bryce Underwood’s legs as well, as anything to test this defense on the ground is worth trying.

When Michigan does go in the air, look for the tight ends to again be a big factor. Getting Marsh back would certainly help in the vertical passing game, but without JJ Buchanan, the big targets seem to be the best way to make it work with Underwood running the offense. I do not expect the Wolverines to score a ton, but some timely third down catches can help sustain drives that are primarily fueled by the run game.

Defense: The good, the bad, and the ugly

Ohio State essentially has one good player, who is theoretically better than the other one good players of the past, though certainly Michigan is not unfamiliar with building a game plan around locking up a star Buckeye receiver. Jeremiah Smith is probably not going to get shut out in his final home game, but the Wolverines need to trust their secondary once again and not allow the offense to hit a bunch of big strikes downfield.

If they can do that, then it is hard to imagine Luke Fahey consistently winning against this defense. The Ohio State backup has been sometimes decent, sometimes bad since coming in for Julian Sayin, and he has now thrown a pick in three straight games. Fahey has not been helped out by his receivers, but this is uncharted waters for the Wolverines, not having to really fear the Buckeye quarterback.

Making matters worse, the run game is just 92nd nationally in YPC, though Bo Jackson has found the end zone five times the last three weeks despite limited yardage. Still, if the plan is for Michigan to win in the trenches, the defensive line should be up for the challenge here, especially after coming off a complete shutdown of Wayne Knight.

The one advantage of playing this game at the Shoe is that the crowd will not be pleased if this game gets ugly, which it very well may. As teams trade punts and passes fall errantly to the ground, Ohio State will get frustrated while the Wolverines enjoy the plan falling into place. The defense has a lot of burden on it this weekend, but that has been the case all season, and the Indiana and UCLA games proved this plan can work — even if the margins are slim.

Embracing chaos

Looking ahead, Michigan does not know who its head coach, quarterback, or even athletic director will be next season; this year was embarrassing and frustrating, and few positives will ever be remembered about 2026. Despite all this, it is Ohio State who comes into this game arguably worse off, enduring its worst season in years and without much certainty for its own future.

That sure sounds like advantage: Michigan to me. Underwood is who he is, but the same could be said for Fahey. While the Wolverines have underperformed on the ground this season, they are definitely the more likely team to have a big jump in production on Saturday. And though the Michigan defense has not been 100 percent reliable all year, it sure looks more promising right now than the Buckeyes’.

I know that Ohio State is nearly a double-digit favorite, and I know this could easily be a loss for Michigan, but after everything that has gone catastrophically wrong this season, it is amazing that the team can enter this game with a reasonable dose of expectation. All of us are ready to forget this year ever happened, but still stealing a win in The Game would be the perfect cap for this chaotic nightmare.

michigan.headline: Fee Fi Foe Film: Ohio State Defense 2026
michigan.body:
Fee Fi Foe Film: Ohio State Defense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 27th, 2026 at 8:34 AM

Previously: Ohio State Offense
Now we move on to the Buckeye defense, a unit that started strong but has degraded over the course of the season. They've allowed over 30 points per game across the last four contests and faith in Columbus in Defensive Coordinator Matt Patricia seems to be wavering some. They will have a far easier task this week against the lowly Michigan offense, but today we'll look at vulnerabilities in this unit:
The Film: OSU's defense has faced a lot of good offenses recently, so I don't really have a comparable unit to Michigan's to watch the Buckeyes face. Maryland's offense was one but that was seven weeks ago and begins to lose relevance in terms of recency. Looking at the last four games, none of USC, Northwestern, Oregon, nor Nebraska are all that useful, but I again went with the Huskers because 1.) it's recent and 2.) Nebraska likes to run the football (and the QB), which is relevant to Michigan. I'm not going to look too closely at other games because the Oregon and USC offenses are way better than Michigan's, though I did chart the Oregon/OSU game earlier, so I have some frame of reference for the Buckeyes.
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

The Buckeye defensive line features a collection of solid but unexceptional defensive ends, starting with Alabama transfer Qua Russaw. The 6'2/244 Russaw is a small end, often in a two-point stance with the ability to drop into coverage. The other side was held by longtime Buckeye Kenyatta Jackson Jr. for most of this season, but Jackson hasn't really flourished into an impact player as a senior despite having prototypical size at 6'6/263. The middling play of Jackson may have led to Zion Grady (6'4/262) taking over the nominal starting job over the past two games. Grady and Jackson are playing essentially the same snap count, though, so it's not a big difference. They're just guys. No other defensive end on this defense is a factor right now, as Beau Atkinson didn't even play against Nebraska.
Defensive tackle is a little more promising. I'm a fan of how former 5* Eddrick Houston is coming along. I don't think he should go pro after this season, but he's an NFL Draft pick in the future, having strung a few really strong games together. Senior Jason Moore wasn't much of a factor in prior seasons but has emerged as a co-starter of sorts alongside UCF transfer John Walker. I like Walker more, but they're both okay. Two more names in the mix are James Smith (another Bama transfer) and Will Smith Jr., who join the mix but weren't distinguishable to me. At defensive tackle, Houston is a guy I like, the rest here are also just guys.
At linebacker, the Buckeyes have suffered an injury in losing starter Christian Alliegro for this game. They do have other LBs with enough seasoning to step in, meaning that Payton Pierce likely steps up at MIKE against Michigan. He's okay, but the LBs in general (with the DBs) had some issues fitting the run against Nebraska. Riley Pettijohn and Tarvos "TJ" Alford round out the second level and given the way Michigan plays, I assume they will be out there quite a bit (with 4-3 as the default personnel package). There's a big drop-off in usage to anyone else on this level but 5* freshman Cincere Johnson is probably LB4 going into tomorrow.
In the secondary, Devin Sanchez was a high 5* in the 2025 class now in his first year of starting at corner and is alright. He pairs with savvy veteran Jermaine Mathews Jr., still a sturdy corner in his own right to man the outside. Neither get the star and neither get the cyan. Freshman Nk Jay Timmons has become an important player for Ohio State's defense and his absence from part of the Nebraska game was felt, so his injury status (Mathews is also questionable) will be important to follow. Other corners include former Wolverine Cam Calhoun and Georgia transfer Dominick Kelly (both haven't played since Oregon), as well as freshman Jordan Thomas, who did have to play a fair bit against Nebraska and didn't look ready.
Safety contains our Dangerman in FSU transfer Earl Little Jr., an excellent all-around free safety who has been a rock at the back of Ohio State's defense this season. He's joined by Jaylen McClain, one of the few returning starters off last year's vaunted defense to give the Buckeyes an admirable safety duo. Simeon Caldwell is another one of the freshmen who have had to see the field for this OSU defense, while Leroy Roker III is a little bit older. Those are your two depth safeties, clear steps down from the starters but not eyesores in my view.
[AFTER THE JUMP: clips]

Base set: As stated, I think Michigan will be using their tight ends more coming off the game we just watched and I think Ohio State will counter by using three linebackers. How they decide to align them is one of the questions. Sometimes it was a normal looking 4-3:

Last year when I looked at OSU, they were using Arvell Reese as their LB/EDGE hybrid allowing them to play a 4-3 that looked like a 5-2. They are still doing that some:

But sometimes they can put two on the line for a 6-man front:

4-2-5 still exists, sometimes looking normal and sometimes putting a linebacker more in the slot:

Things did get funky on occasion. They ran some 3-3-5 with two LBs on the line so it looked like 5-1:

And here's a 3-2-6 look (with the LBs rolled down):

As well as 6 DL:

The Matt Patricia was an NFL Guy thing can be seen through this.
Pressure: Last year I didn't chart Ohio State as terribly blitzy, checking in around 27% for rushing >4 defenders on a given play. This year it's far higher, at nearly 40%. Nebraska ran the ball a lot and Ohio State was eager to load up the box and fire their defenders downhill, which led to more run blitzes but also success for the Huskers rolling Anthony Collandrea out on bootlegs and designed QB runs. On the flip side, OSU rushed <4 on 17% of snaps last season and that held up as a high percentage this year, checking in at a nearly identical 16%. Again, lots of different personnel packages, formations, and numbers of defenders rushing the QB.
Man or zone coverage: Last year I said the following about Ohio State's coverage, while I was doing my gag of calling Patricia various villains of cinema names:
Man or zone coverage: Both man and zone for Ohio State. René Belloq Patricia is running a lot of single high coverages this year, Cover 1 and Cover 3 to allow Caleb Downs to slide into the box and affect the run game and rush the passer on occasion. There's also been some QQH and with Downs' and Reese's ability to move around the formation, Col. Kurtz Patricia is able to disguise coverages well. The advantage of having the ole "NFL DC", with all malice of the quotation marks delivered with intention.

Statistically, this was a Cover 3 defense last year, though he was known in the NFL for running a lot of Cover 1 in Detroit. I don't see a ton of change this year, still plenty of man and then you get the safety rotation and plenty of zone in there too.
Dangerman: Let's take a look at S Earl Little Jr. today with this section. Little was one of my top graded players from the Nebraska game and it's always a joy when that lines up with what PFF has been seeing. Little is the highest graded starter among Ohio State's defenders and he's one of the top 40 highest graded safeties in college football this season nationally. Little's game against Nebraska wasn't terribly flashy, but he popped up repeatedly making nice plays out in space:

Here he is in the run game, dipping around a block and making a stop:

I also liked this play laying the boom to jar the ball free:

Here are some season highlights:

The latest projection from the consensus big board over at Pro Football Network has Little at 163, which feels a bit low for me (fellow S Jaylen McClain, who is also good, is far higher!). He's a draftable player to me, having been a solid performer at Florida State last year too (4 INTs). One of a few options for the Dangerman but Little is who I went with.

Overview
Last season's Ohio State defense was a marvel. They allowed 130 total points across 14 regular season games, ceding 20+ points once, in the season ending defeat to Miami. Of course, that game included a Julian Sayin pick six, so you can't even pin seven of those points on the defense. They were an astonishingly great unit in Matt Patricia's first season, one that dismayed Lions fans like myself who wish nothing but misery for the rest of Patricia's career as a football coach.
Of course, one may have remarked that Patricia was, to some extent, playing checkers against a Doberman. He had three first round picks (all top 11 picks) and five 1st/2nd round picks at his disposal. Seven players in total were drafted off that defense in the 2026 NFL Draft. The board was tilted in Patricia's favor, as Ohio State was obscenely talented and had better players than everyone they went up against. He also had a unit that he was inheriting from Jim Knowles, who has a very strong body of work despite some of the criticisms of him. Knowles was swept up in the end of the James Franklin regime last year in State College but this year has landed in Knoxville and transformed Tennessee's defense almost instantly, from allowing 28.8 PPG in 2025 to 14.2 PPG in 2026. Knowles also had success turning around a unit with Oklahoma State before going to Columbus.
I think Knowles is clearly a good defensive coordinator. Patricia took over a defense Knowles had just coached to the nation's best scoring defense in 2024 and kept the car on the road, with the players to out-talent anyone he faced. This year things got a little tougher. All those studs departed and as I remarked in the summer, the replacements weren't always obvious. Gaps in the depth chart meant it was portal time and some freshmen took the field.
The result is a unit that is lacking the star power of a year ago. Against lesser opponents in the first half of the season, Ohio State's defense held strong, allowing 3 to Ball State and Kent State, 14 to Iowa, and 16 to Maryland. Illinois got to 19 points on 462 yards (6.5 YPP) as an early warning sign, while Texas had a harder time to 24 points (336 yards, 4.3 YPP). Even the Indiana game was a fairly impressive showing, though it was one that began to puncture the aura around that Hoosier offense in my eyes, as the Buckeyes held IU to 15 points on the road. 369 yards on 5.3 YPP was a little bit better under the hood, but this still looked like a very strong defense.
Then the last four weeks happened. Against a series of opponents who have respectable offenses, things have quickly gone south. Ohio State is allowing over 30 PPG across those four games, as well as a 5.4 YPP clip in that span. The Nebraska game that I charted was not even as bad as some of these performances have been but there were still worrying signs. One of the bigger issues underpinning this defensive issue is what I mentioned at the start of the last paragraph: they don't have the stars of 2025. There are no Caleb Downs, Arvell Reese, or Sonny Styles on this defense. They have a lot of guys who are fine but I was struggling to discern true difference makers when I was reviewing the tape.
Besides Earl Little, the one other guy I do really like is Eddrick Houston, the 5* junior DT who is starting to round into his own:

Houston's run stuffing ability is becoming more real and as a whole, the run defense hasn't been the big issue. Opponents haven't been able to post big YPC clips against the Buckeyes even over this span, though Nebraska was very interested in testing it out and did highlight some vulnerabilities. Nebraska finished with 44 rush attempts compared to 28 pass attempts (+1 sack) and with Anthony Collandrea in the run game, they were trying to hammer away at OSU. Some of it worked and some didn't. The biggest warning I saw for Ohio State was poor play from the back seven when creases opened up front:

Not good up front as Kenyatta Jackson and John Walker are discarded, creating a run lane and Christian Alliegro fails to find it. Alliegro won't be playing tomorrow due to injury, but this was a problem across the LB level and it bled into the secondary some. Payton Pierce will likely be taking his spot and was an issue on this one:
MLB #26

As someone who was scrolling corners of the Buckeye interwebs during the late stages of the Nebraska game, I saw chatter from certain places dismayed at the issues fitting the run.
I also don't know how this play worked to seal the game. Twice in a row on the final drive to clinch the game, Nebraska faced a 3rd down (first was 3rd & 2, this was 3rd & 5) and both times they did the same thing, PA boot with Collandrea under center, then he runs for the first down. The first one is a nice play against Ohio State's tendencies to be overaggressive in the box against the run, but the second one working right after is malpractice:

So, maybe that's something to put down on the sheet. Still, it wasn't all bad. The Huskers got OSU early on with high safeties leading to light boxes but once Patricia countered by loading up, there were plenty of times it was tough sledding:

If Michigan is going to try and battering ram their way without much creativity outside the tackles or threat of the pass, I expect OSU to be comfortable loading up and stopping it, even if they will occasionally blow one for a chunk gain. Getting Underwood involved is going to be important and I think there are some positive signs from the Nebraska tape that you could take away in that domain.
The pass game has been more fruitful for opposing offenses against this defense. Here are the last four games:
Jayden Maiava: 15/22, 222, 10.1, 1 TD, 0 INT
Dylan Raiola: 25/40, 257, 6.4, 2 TD, 0 INT
Nicco Marichol: 18/31, 225, 7.3, 1 TD, 0 INT
Collandrea: 19/28, 200, 7.1, 3 TD, 0 INT
Marichol is NW's backup, so he's somewhat interesting for this, while the other three QBs are several orders of magnitude better than Bryce Underwood. What stands out to me from those numbers mostly is the goose egg in the interception column. Opponents have thrown just four interceptions against the OSU defense this season and one of those was the goofiest, most unearned INT in history in the Texas game. Hank Brown of Iowa on October 3 was the last QB to throw an interception against the Buckeye defense(!!) and he is one of just two P4 QBs to throw a pick against OSU, with that Arch blooper reel INT being the other.
So, that's an issue. As it pertains to the Nebraska game, the Huskers were able to move the ball through the air as you can see from that statline, but I didn't always think that coverage was that "bad". Jordan Thomas probably isn't ready for the big time yet at corner but this wasn't awful from him, just a great pitch and catch against pure man coverage after Patricia shows his hand:

Jermaine Mathews Jr. was beaten on a slant here before S Leroy Roker III could arrive but it still requires a good ball from Collandrea:

Seeing the kind of passing success that Nebraska was having made me a little more pessimistic, in that I don't think Michigan, as it stands, has the QB play (or possibly receiver ammo) to replicate that. There weren't many coverage busts and I don't think that Mathews nor Devin Sanchez are bad. The Nk Jay Timmons has also become an important part of this defense, an excellent cover guy out of the slot as a freshman. And obviously I'm a fan of Little over the top + Jaylen McClain. The personnel here on the back-end isn't bad and there was plenty of good coverage in this game:

I will be curious to see the matchups in terms of who is covering Michigan's newfound tight ends and what you can do with that, as Nebraska didn't use them for much other than running them underneath (which was effective):

Finally, when we look at pass rush, I do not see the defensive end abilities of old. An Ohio State that once had the Bosas, Chase Young, even Jack Sawyer 2024 version... not quite what I see here. Qua Russaw, Zion Grady, and Jackson are just sort of guys. They are fine and can probably have success against Michigan's OL situation but they don't scare me in the aggregate. The response from Patricia is to get funky and toss all kinds of blitzes and sim pressures at the opposition, coming from all places and dropping eight with frequency. Sometimes it works:

And against Michigan's front, it probably can work since it's a young and inexperienced group. I don't see it as a major obstacle against the median team, however. Quarterbacks have had enough time to work and they've found holes in the Ohio State defense. Combined with some chunks in the run game, it's been enough for good offenses to do damage. Don't get your hopes too up, though, as Michigan doesn't exactly have a good offense...

What does this mean for Michigan?
Uh, idk. We don't really know what actually matters for Michigan at this point. The Wolverines did a few things right against UCLA (Savion Hiter looked good!) but they didn't consistently string together long drives. They had three total drives of 40+ yards, which is progress but isn't exactly winning you many games if your defense isn't dominating and you're winning the field position battle. I don't know if Ohio State's defense, in its current state and engagement level, is as strong as UCLA's, but I don't think it's awful either. There are enough decent players here that I wouldn't expect them to allow Michigan's offense to achieve something they couldn't all season besides against UTEP and Rutgers.
Instead, I'd see it as more of the same. Michigan may rip off a big run or two if OSU shows the same issues fitting the run that they did last week and Bryce Underwood may fire his weekly good couple of passes. But the Wolverines haven't earned our trust enough to think they will have a good day, even against a defense licking its wounds. They will have to show us something, that Kyle Whittingham did actually understand the rivalry and the Michigan offense has a few scripted plays up their sleeves. That, combined with one of those good days from Underwood, combined with a poor effort by the OSU defense, combined with Michigan's defense coaxing mistakes out of Fahey, are the ingredients for another 13-10 (and I'm not talking about last night's Bills game). It wouldn't be pretty and there's no reason for the Buckeyes to let it happen. But the weird vibes on both sides make me refuse to rule it out.
Reluctantly, I say Beat Ohio.

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The Rutgers Scarlet Knights
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MI - NOVEMBER 20: Michigan State Spartans safety Jonathan Granby (17) and linebacker Caleb Wheatland (44) tackle Oregon Ducks running back Da'Jaun Riggs (21) after a short gain during a college football game between the Michigan State Spartans and Oregon Ducks on November 20, 2026 at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing, MI. (Photo by Adam Ruff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Happy Friday, TOC Nation.  Hope you all enjoyed Thanksgiving.  Tomorrow is the final game of the 2026 football season.  This game is for the indignity of last place, so we do have something to cheer for and reason to hope for a win.  I sat down with Andrew Rice from On The Banks for a little Q&A. Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: This is year 7 of Greg Schiano’s 2nd stint as Rutgers head coach. Last year, the Scarlet Knights were 5-7. You are 3-8 coming into the final game of the season. What were your expectations coming into this season? What has been the biggest reason for those expectations being met or not met? Is there any possibility that this will be Schiano’s last game as Rutgers’ coach?

Andrew Rice:  My expectations for this season were 6-6 with a bowl bid or 5-7 just missing out on a bowl game.  I was expecting an improvement on defense under new coordinator Travis Johansen, and that just hasn’t happened to the level it needed to. On top of that, the quarterback play unexpectedly regressed severely and when the team’s initial starter, Dylan Lonergan, was finally starting to find a groove, he was knocked out for several games due to injury. Backup AJ Surace, who competed with Lonergan for the starting job in training camp, had his best game of the season against Penn State last week, so the hope is he has started to turn the corner. As for Schiano getting fired, our AD, Keli Zinn, already confirmed he will be back for 2027.

TOC: Dylan Lonergan was your quarterback to begin the season, but he was knocked out of your 7th game of the season and has not been back since. He also missed your week 2 game with another injury. In his absence, AJ Surace has been the guy under center. Rutgers was 2-4 before the injury, lost the game the injury occurred in, and is 1-3 since after a win at Penn State this past weekend. What is the difference between Lonergan and Surace? Has Surace gotten better since becoming the starter? What are his strengths and weaknesses?

AR: Lonergan was much more experienced than Surace; otherwise, they were a very similar build of quarterback. Surace’s best game since taking over was against the Nittany Lions, so we still have to see if that’s consistent improvement or a one-off. As for his best qualities, he has shown flashes of being able to hit the deep ball, so that is something to look for.

TOC: Who are the offensive skill players that could put up some numbers against MSU? Do you have any future NFL players that Spartan fans should get to know?

AR: This is normally where I would say wide receiver KJ Duff, but since he is out for the season, I will say running back Antwan Raymond, who is currently leading the Big Ten in rushing yards this season.

TOC: What is your defensive base formation? Which level of the defense is its best? Who is the one player the MSU coaching staff must prepare for?

AR: Rutgers typically runs a 4-2-5, four down linemen, two linebackers, two corners, and three safeties. One of those safeties is listed on the Knights roster as a ‘STUD,’ which is typically a safety-linebacker hybrid. The Knights’ linebackers really stepped up last game, while players like EDGE Sekou Kromah and LB Sean Allison made their presence felt and could be two guys to look out for.

TOC: Fill in the blank: Rutgers will win if ____________.  Rutgers will lose if ____________.

AR: Rutgers will win if their defense plays the way it did against Penn State. Rutgers will lose if their defense plays the way it did earlier in the season.

TOC: Predict the final score.

TC: Michigan State’s offense does not strike me as very potent, especially when factoring in their injuries at quarterback. Surace has had more time to adjust to his role and should be more confident after having a good game last game. While both teams might have to slog it out, Rutgers’ offense will break through first to secure the win. Rutgers 24, Michigan State 17.

TOC: Bonus question.  Aside from former athletes, who is Rutgers’ most famous alum?

TC: This one is very interesting! I would have to say James Gandolfini. For those who don’t know, he played Tony in The Sopranos. This answer could be biased, though, as I am rewatching the show right now.

msu.headline: Michigan State Gets Past Arkansas, 70-67
msu.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 26: Jeremy Fears Jr. #1 and Kur Teng #2 of the Michigan State Spartans celebrate following a made three point basket basket from Teng during the second half against the Arkansas Razorbacks in the CBS Thanksgiving Classic at Little Caesars Arena on November 26, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Jaime Crawford/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Michigan State Spartans and the Arkansas Razorbacks gave the fans a highly entertaining back-and-forth game on Thanksgiving.  I will get to the game in a minute, but first I am going to talk a bit about something that Tom Izzo mentioned at the beginning of his post-game press conference, and that is the Detroit Lions game.

Fortunately for me, I live about five minutes from Little Caesars arena so I was able to watch the entirety of the Lions game before darting over for the MSU game.  I only missed the first five minutes of the action at LCA.  But the end of that Lions game ruined my entire day.  And I have to call into question Coach Dan Campbell’s strategy on that last defensive effort.  Up three with less than two minutes to go, the best-case scenario is that the Lions would have held the Bears to a field goal.  A touchdown, obviously, would be the worst case.  With the Bears down to one timeout, they certainly were limited in how many plays they would be able to run.  And yet, Coach Campbell helped out the visiting team by using two of his own timeouts.  His thought process was that they would be able to hold them to a field goal and then have time left for the offense to do something.  But this was not the time to play for the best-case scenario; he should have been more focused on avoiding the worst possible chain of events.  Had the Lions not called those two timeouts, Chicago would not have had time for those last two shots at the end zone and they would have had to settle for kicking a field goal right after D’Andre Swift ran it down to the 3-yard line.  That is my rant.  I think it was a case of poor end-of-game clock management on Campbell’s part.  That was a game that the Lions should have at the very least been able to get to overtime.  Chicago never should have had that many opportunities to score at the end.

Now that I got that out of the way, let’s talk about MSU and Arkansas.  By the time I got to my spot along the baseline, the game was about five minutes in.  The first half was not the most impressive display of basketball by either team.  Both sides struggled to put the ball through the net from all distances.  Neither team was able to build much momentum.  The largest lead by either side in the first 20 minutes was a 6-point advantage for Arkansas, but that only happened after a long stretch of MSU not scoring rather than Arkansas getting a few in a row.  MSU did manage to swing the game back the other way, briefly going up by four with a little over 5 minutes to go.  But Arkansas closed the half on an 11-3 run to take a 4-point lead to the locker room.

The Razorbacks pushed the lead up to 8 at the beginning of the 2nd half before MSU began to chip away.  To Arkansas’ credit, they did a good job of responding whenever MSU would get two baskets in a row, preventing the Spartans from getting on a run.  At the 11:20 mark, MSU finally tied the game up, and they took the lead on their next possession.

Once MSU took the lead, they never looked back as they proceeded to go on a 14-4 run for a 64-51 lead with just under 5 to play.  The end of that run featured three consecutive triples from Kur Teng.  In the final minute and change, though, Arkansas clawed back with some assistance from some suddenly cold MSU shooting.  Getting to within 8 with 1:03 on the clock, the Razorbacks then forced a turnover, got to the line, made the first, missed the second, got the rebound, and eventually hit a triple to get to within 4 with 26 ticks left.  After a pair of Jeremy Fears FTs pushed it back to 6, Arkansas responded with an and-1 to get within 3.  Fears was fouled with 8 seconds remaining, but he missed the front end, leaving Arkansas with a chance to tie it with a triple.  Arkansas raced down the floor and got off a good-looking shot that nearly went down but decided to pop out at the last moment, and MSU held on for the victory.

You can rewatch the ending in these highlights.

View Link

Both teams had one thing they excelled at and one thing they did rather poorly.  For Arkansas, they won the rebounding competition, 39-36.  The Razorbacks had 17 offensive rebounds.  After the game, Izzo called MSU getting outrebounded “unamerican.”  On the negative side, Arkansas went 3-23 on three-point attempts, or 13%.  I am sure some of you are thinking to yourselves that they could have won if they had just gone 5-23, which is still only 21.7%.  But MSU also had their struggles in one particular aspect.  The Spartans shot 8-18 from the free-throw line.  That 44% included four missed front ends on 1-and-1 opportunities.  Even the normally reliable Fears only went 6-10.  To negate the awful display from the charity stripe, MSU was nearly automatic from downtown, admittedly on low volume, drilling 8 of their 12 tries.  As mentioned before, Teng hit three in a row at one point, which were his only attempts.  Jordan Scott was 3-5 and Fears made both of his tries.

The game ended how it should have, with the team that was dominant for most of the game holding on for the win, very much unlike the Lions game.  MSU is now 6-1 and has six days off before playing their Big Ten opener against Minnesota at home.

VICTORY FOR MSU!

msu.headline: We Have Come to the End
msu.body:
A wide shot of the exterior of SHI Stadium, the home field of the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, before an NCAA FBS football game in Piscataway, United States, on October 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

Well, TOC, here we are.  At the end of another difficult football season, in this situation:

Michigan State has to beat Rutgers, on the road (Saturday, 4:15 PM ET, Big Ten Network), to earn a tie for last place in the 18-team Big Ten Conference.  They will be tasked with doing so, perhaps without their first and second string quarterbacks, and numerous other key players on both sides of the ball.

This article gets published before the first required football availability report, which comes out later tonight, but MSU QB Alessio Milivojevic took a hard hit to his left side / left arm two games ago against Washington.  He was seen on the sideline Friday against Oregon wearing a substantial brace.  I have no idea what specific type of injury this would be supporting, but it just seems unlikely that it would heal up in time for Saturday.

On top of all this, the Spartans are coming off a 45-7 beatdown at the hands of Oregon while Rutgers is riding high after a 25-24 win over Penn State, their first in Happy Valley since 1988.

Ok, this is enough negativity for one article.  Let’s look for some positives.

While the Spartans’ record and standing in the Big Ten has not improved this year, things still feel different.  MSU has responded to bad losses early in the season to Nebraska and Wisconsin.  They’ve continued to play hard and came up just short to Illinois, Northwestern, and Washington.  Regardless of what happens on Saturday in New Jersey, the season will be most remembered for the win at Michigan, which showed the culture and style of play Pat Fitzgerald is trying to recreate at MSU.

However, it would still be nice to build off the UM win with something other than a close loss to Washington.  That will hopefully come via a solid transfer portal haul in January but a win at Rutgers certainly wouldn’t hurt MSU as they plan their portal possibilities.

In 2024, under Jonathan Smith, Michigan State had a nice 32-20 win against Iowa in mid-October and then a real chance to win at Michigan the following Saturday.  The Spartans blew that chance in Ann Arbor and then got blown out by Indiana and Illinois.  The season ended with a 41-14 home loss to Rutgers that kept the Spartans from bowl eligibility and was every bit as bad as the score would indicate.

Many might argue that the final nail in Smith’s coffin at MSU was the 2025 Homecoming loss to UCLA but perhaps it all started by failing to capitalize on that Iowa win two years ago.

I don’t know if the Spartans will win at Rutgers on Saturday but I also don’t see this season ending like it did in 2024.  Michigan State will, once again, come to play.  A victory might hinge on if third string quarterback Kayd Coffman can stay consistent, manage a whole game, and avoid turnovers.  We’ll look at keys to the game at the end but first, let’s take a closer look at how Rutgers compares to MSU.
