Rutgers Season Recap

Until Saturday’s win at Penn State, Rutgers’ only two victories were on September 25 against Howard, 58-7, and 37-30 at Maryland on October 17.

Comparing common opponents with MSU, Rutgers has lost at Northwestern (42-14), to Michigan (28-21), at Wisconsin (31-10), and to Nebraska (31-0).  Overall, Michigan State has fared slightly better against these teams.

Offensive Comparison

Rutgers may also have questions at quarterback coming into this game.  Boston College transfer Dylan Lonergan started the season but went out with a concussion in the October 24 loss at Northwestern and has not played since.  Lonergan was listed as questionable for the Penn State game but did not see the field.

The Knights stuck with junior signal called AJ Surace, who managed the game effectively against PSU.  He completed 24 of 39 passes for 178 yards, a touchdown, and no turnovers.  These numbers may not pop out but they’re not bad against a PSU defense that ranks first in the Big Ten in allowing just 151.5 yards per game through the air.  Surace also played well in the loss to Wisconsin, going 14-24 for 161 yards and a TD but struggled mightily against Northwestern, Michigan, and Nebraska.  Surace’s completion percentage in these three games was well under 50%.

For the season, Surace is completing 53.8% of his passes for 1025 yards on 6.5 yards per attempt, nine touchdowns, and seven interceptions.  Longergan is at 58.3% for 1066 yards on 8.3 yards per attempt, 10 TDs, and six picks.

Rutgers, however, like Michigan State, is a run-first team.  The Scarlett Knights have stuck to the ground on 56% of their plays this season but have managed just 3.8 yards per carry and 134.1 yards per game – good for 12th in the Big Ten.  For comparison, MSU is 16th with 106.5 yards per game on an abysmal 2.9 yards per carry.

Two primary backs lead Rutgers’ rushing attack.  Junior Antwan Raymond has gone for 911 yards and eight TDs on 4.9 yards per carry.  Sophomore Louisiana Tech transfer Clay Thevenin backs up with Raymond and has added 524 yards and five TDs on five YPC.

Overall on offense, Rutgers is 15th in the Big Ten with 23.4 points per game while MSU is dead last at just 17.7.  So, first team to three touchdowns has a good chance of winning this one.

Defensive Comparison

Rutgers seems to employ a base 4-2-5 defense and benefits from a pair of solid linebackers. Senior transfer from Drake Sean Allison and fellow senior Moses Walker anchor the middle of the Rutgers D and lead the team in tackles.

Overall though, Rutgers has struggled on defense in giving up 31.5 points per game this year, which ranks ahead of only Purdue in the Big Ten.  After giving up 45 to Oregon, Michigan State slipped a bit to 15th in the league at 25.3 PPG.

MSU’s D has been much better against the run in allowing 137.8 yards per game while Rutgers gives up 188.  With Jaziun Patterson returning to play against Oregon and Brandon Tullis finding some momentum in recent games, hopefully the Spartan run game can take advantage in this one and support whichever QB ends up under center for Michigan State.

The Spartan D, even if several key players remain out or limited by injury, should also provide an advantage in the pass game.  Rutgers gives up 223.2 yards per game in the air while Michigan State is tenth in the conference in allowing 206.5.  If Surace plays and MSU can just limit him to what he did at Penn State, then it could bode well for a Michigan State victory.

Keys to the Game for MSU

Penalties, Mistakes, and Near Misses.  After doing well to really limit penalties earlier in the season, they are starting to mount for MSU.  In their last four games, the Spartans had averaged 7.5 flags for 70 yards.  On top of the penalties, two key turnovers really hurt against Washington.  A muffed punt and other special teams errors made the Oregon game worse.  Finally, a couple of downfield passes that just missed against Washington hurt the Spartans’ efforts in that game.

The penalties might be a result of playing so many less-experienced backup players but, for all their efforts, this team just isn’t good enough to overcome so many mistakes.  Even though Rutgers has also experienced a tough season, Michigan State is going to need a clean game to win.

Quarterback Consistency.  Here, we’ll assume freshman Kayd Coffman gets his third start for MSU.  His first two have come against two of the Big Ten’s best teams in UCLA and Oregon.  It would be nice to see what Coffman can do against a team where MSU might be a little more evenly-matched.

At UCLA, Coffman completed his first four passes, with one going for a touchdown, as the Spartans took a 7-0 lead in that game.  Then, he went 0-6 with a crucial pick in Bruin territory before giving way to Leo Hannan.

Against the Ducks, Coffman missed on his first three attempts, then completed nine of his next 10, but went 1-6 with another interception the rest of the way before again giving way to Hannan.

Coffman maintaining a consistent output at Rutgers – say 15-23 for 170 yards, a TD, and no picks – and Patterson, Tullis, and the offensive line taking advantage of the Knights’ poor run defense to take some pressure off Coffman, could send the Spartans into portal season with a victory and some positive momentum.

Regardless of what happens Saturday, TOC, thanks for reading this previews.  Hopefully next year, we can look forward to them a little more.

msu.headline: Michigan State Film Room: A Duck Hunt Gone Horribly Wrong
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: The Michigan State Spartans offense lines up against the Oregon Ducks defense during the first half of a college football game at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. The Oregon Ducks won the game 45-7. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

For those of you who spent the weekend playing GTA 6 instead of watching Michigan State football, you didn’t miss much. If you stripped away the uniforms and logos on Friday night, you might have thought you were watching a MAC team collecting a paycheck against one of college football’s powerhouses. The talent disparity between Michigan State and Oregon was that glaring. In my opinion, this was the Spartans’ worst performance of the season, and the 45-7 final score was a fair reflection of what transpired on the field.

As I discussed in my recent article on NIL spending, the Ducks’ estimated football roster budget is more than double that of Michigan State. Oregon was bigger, faster, stronger and deeper than MSU, and it showed.

The Ducks more than doubled MSU in total offense (422 to 205 yards), averaged 4.9 yards per carry to MSU’s 2.3 and converted 67% of their third downs. Michigan State won the time of possession battle and got a solid performance from its punter, but beyond that, it was slim pickings for positives.

I wish there was more to highlight from this game, but everyone saw the bad, and we don’t need another Film Room pointing out the obvious.

This week, we’ll take a closer look at what young quarterback Kayd Coffman showed in his second collegiate start and a couple of encouraging plays from redshirt freshman running back Jace Clarizio. We’ll also examine Oregon’s fake field goal and why the overmatched Spartans should have been taking more chances on special teams.

Let’s dive into the film!

Kayd Coffman: A Trial by Fire

As I pointed out over the weekend, it’s hard to imagine a more daunting set of circumstances for a true freshman quarterback making his first two collegiate starts. Coffman drew No. 9 UCLA and No. 13 Oregon, two teams I believe could legitimately win a national championship this season. The College Football Playoff looks wide open without a clear-cut favorite.

I could easily see five players from Oregon’s defense alone being selected in the first three rounds of the 2027 NFL draft: defensive tackles A’Mauri Washington and Bear Alexander, edge defenders Matayo Uiagalelei and Teitum Tuioti, and safety Koi Perich. That’s a significant challenge for any quarterback, let alone a true freshman.

Coffman completed 10 of 19 passes for 106 yards with no touchdowns and one interception. He was sacked just once. Nothing about that stat line jumps off the page, but I thought Coffman held his own considering the caliber of competition he faced. For the most part, he avoided putting his team in difficult situations and, at times, displayed a level of composure well beyond his years.

Two plays against Oregon caught my attention and deserve a closer look.

PLAY 1: Coffman Baits the Ducks

Late in the first quarter, Michigan State appeared to have converted a 3rd-and-1, but an illegal shift penalty on tight end Kai Rios negated the first down. Instead of moving the chains, the Spartans found themselves facing a much more difficult 3rd-and-6 against an aggressive Oregon defensive front.

With the Ducks looking to pin their ears back and get after the quarterback, Kayd Coffman (No. 10) manufactures a free play. Using a savvy fake snap with his hands, likely accompanied by a hard count, Coffman draws Oregon outside linebacker Nasir Wyatt (No. 31) offside.

What I also love about this play is the awareness both Coffman and Fredrick Moore (No. 6) display in recognizing the flag and getting on the same page. Watch Moore at the bottom of the screen. He appears to adjust his original route, and the two essentially start playing backyard football, something I hope many of us will be doing this Thanksgiving. Throw the ball up in the vicinity of your receiver and give him an opportunity to come down with it.

There could have been a defensive holding penalty called on this play as well, but Moore still manages to make an incredible one-handed catch along the left sideline. The concentration, coordination and body control required to make that catch are exceptional. As spectacular as the catch was, don’t overlook the football IQ both players displayed.

PLAY 2: Losing the Moments That Matter

After picking up three yards on 3rd-and-6, Michigan State finds itself facing a manageable 4th-and-3 at the Oregon 28-yard line. I have no issue with the decision to go for it here, and I actually really like the play call. Unfortunately, this is another example of Michigan State failing to execute in a pivotal moment.

One of the biggest improvements I want to see from Michigan State next season is its ability to execute when it matters most. Watching the ESPN docuseries “Saban”, I was intrigued by the performance philosophy Nick Saban developed with the help of psychiatrist Dr. Lonny Rosen, nicknamed “The Wizard.” Football is a 60-minute game often decided by a handful of crucial moments, and far too often this season, the Spartans have lost those moments.

Michigan State lines up in a bunch formation with running back Kenneth Williams (No. 32) going in motion from left to right before running a wheel route. Bryson Williams (No. 14) appears to run a deep post route, while Chrishon McCray (No. 13), Samson Gash (No. 5) and tight end Carson Gulker (No. 12) run inbreaking routes designed to find the soft spots in Oregon’s zone coverage.

Credit to offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan for dialing up a good combination of zone-beater routes against this Oregon defense. I really like how the three receivers form a triangle in the middle of the field, stretching the underneath defenders horizontally and vertically while giving Coffman multiple passing options at or beyond the first-down marker.

The offensive line blocks this play up well, and Coffman has plenty of room to pick up the first down with his legs. Watch right tackle Rakeem Johnson (No. 55) recognize Coffman starting to scramble and put himself in position to potentially deliver a block downfield.

An accurate throw or a successful scramble likely moves the chains here. Instead, the turf monster gets Coffman, resulting in a three-yard loss and a turnover on downs. Did former michigan linebacker Devin Bush sneak into Spartan Stadium the night before the game and leave us another divot? Somebody might want to check the security footage.

Look at Coffman’s eyes at the end of this play. He’s looking around in disbelief. Good decision, good scheme, good blocking and multiple opportunities to convert. Instead of extending the drive and potentially putting a touchdown on the board, Michigan State walks away empty-handed. Just another painful missed opportunity in a season full of them.

Why Wasn’t This Us?

What pains me most about Oregon’s successful fake field goal is that it should have been Michigan State pulling tricks out of the playbook. When you’re as overmatched as the Spartans were on Friday night, stealing an extra possession or extending a drive through a trick play can help neutralize some of that talent disparity.

PLAY 3: Oregon’s Fake Field Goal

Oregon is leading 10-0 with just seven seconds remaining before halftime and no timeouts. Facing a 2nd-and-10, the Ducks line up for a 33-yard field goal, and Pat Fitzgerald even calls a timeout before the snap. Watch Oregon’s kicker Gage Hurych (No. 97), holder Bailey Ettridge (No. 39) and tight end Jamari Johnson (No. 9) on the left side.

This is a beautifully designed fake by Oregon. Ettridge takes the snap and flips it to Hurych, who races around the left edge. However, watch Johnson at the point of attack. He appears to grab Michigan State linebacker Dion Crawford (No. 18) and take him to the ground. To me, that’s a pretty obvious missed holding penalty.

I’d love to have a better angle of Nikai Martinez (No. 21) and Tre Bell (No. 3) rushing off the edge of the field goal formation. Both appear to sell out for the block, leaving the perimeter vulnerable. Given the game situation, I’d much rather see one of those defenders maintain outside leverage than have both aggressively pursue a blocked field goal. I don’t know their exact assignments, but I’d be curious to know who was responsible for outside containment.

The missed holding call doesn’t excuse what happens next. Cam Stodghill (No. 12) has an opportunity to stop Hurych, but the kicker is running like Derrick Henry, with Stodghill bouncing right off him! We’re talking about a placekicker here. Crawford deserves credit for recognizing the fake almost immediately and reacting to the ball, only to be taken out of the play by his own teammate.

What makes this play particularly frustrating is the game situation. If Michigan State tackles Hurych inbounds short of the end zone and the clock expires, Oregon doesn’t even get three points. Instead of heading into the locker room trailing 10-0, Michigan State suddenly finds itself down 17-0.

Despite a solid punting performance from Rhys Dakin, it was a rough night for special teams coordinator LeVar Woods and his unit between Oregon’s successful fake field goal and the muffed punt by Chrishon McCray. When you’re already at a significant disadvantage on offense and defense, you can’t afford to lose the special teams battle, too. I miss the creativity and calculated risks from the program that once gave us Little Giants and Mousetrap.

The Hometown Kid Shows Some Flashes

Coming into the season, Jace Clarizio was a name I frequently heard from Michigan State fans who were eager to see what the young running back could do. The East Lansing High School product was the consensus No. 1 running back prospect in Michigan in the 2025 recruiting class and a four-star recruit according to ESPN. Clarizio gave Spartan fans quite the scare when he flipped his commitment to Alabama on Nov. 26, 2024, only to flip back and sign with Michigan State eight days later on national signing day. His father, Craig Johnson, played for George Perles and was a member of the 1988 Rose Bowl championship team. Between his hometown roots and family ties to the program, Clarizio is an easy guy to root for.

Given his recruiting pedigree, I found it interesting that the redshirt freshman entered the season seemingly sixth on the running back depth chart behind Cam Edwards, Jaziun Patterson, Marvis Parrish, Kenneth Williams and Brandon Tullis.

With injuries thinning out Michigan State’s running back room, we’re finally getting an opportunity to see more of the local kid. Clarizio (No. 25) recorded all six of his touches on Michigan State’s final offensive possession against Oregon, finishing with five carries for 17 yards and one reception for 12 yards.

Let’s take a closer look at two of those plays and what the redshirt freshman brings to the Spartans’ offense.

PLAY 4: From the Flat to a First Down

Late in the fourth quarter, it’s time to get some of the young guys on the field. We have Pope Leo himself, Leo Hannan (No. 15), in at quarterback and Clarizio lined up behind the tight end, off the line of scrimmage to the right of the formation.

Michigan State lines up in a bunch formation, giving the Spartans additional bodies near the line of scrimmage to chip defenders or help with pass protection. Oregon has eight defenders in the box, all relatively close to the line of scrimmage, likely anticipating a run.

There’s no pre-snap motion, and Michigan State releases three pass catchers to the left and two to the right, stretching Oregon’s defense horizontally. Credit to Sheridan for dialing up a good play for a young quarterback against this defensive look. It’s a simple half-field read for Hannan, with Samson Gash running a curl route and Clarizio releasing into the flat.

Oregon brings an overload blitz to the right side of Michigan State’s offensive formation, sending outside linebacker Dutch Horisk (No. 41) and defensive back Aaron Scott Jr. (No. 14), who initially lined up across from Gash and Clarizio. Hannan makes the correct read and gets the ball out quickly, although Scott appears to get a fingertip on the pass with his long reach.

What I like about Clarizio here is his concentration in bringing in this wobbly duck. A lot of young players get excited when they see that much open space in front of them and start running before securing the football. Clarizio makes sure to complete the catch before turning upfield and going to work.

Once Clarizio turns upfield, he makes Oregon linebacker Cruz Rushing (No. 34) look like he just hit a patch of Michigan black ice. A quick change of direction leaves Rushing grasping at air. Clarizio turns a simple pass into the flat into a 12-yard gain, all coming after the catch. That ability to create yards on his own is something this offense has desperately needed.

PLAY 5: Making Plays in Space

As much as I liked what Clarizio showed on the previous play, I liked this one even better. On the very next snap, the redshirt freshman showcases a little more of his elusiveness on what ends up being Michigan State’s longest run of the night.

Facing a 1st-and-15, Michigan State runs a classic zone-read concept to the right side of the formation. Watch redshirt freshman wide receiver Charles Taplin (No. 19). He initially lines up on the right, motions left behind the line of scrimmage before reversing direction and coming back to the right to serve as a lead blocker for Clarizio.

Oregon lines up in a 4-3 defensive front with its linebackers playing close to the line of scrimmage, seemingly anticipating a run. At the snap, the linebackers follow their keys and flow toward the football. Oregon simply has more defenders than Michigan State has blockers on the play side, leaving Clarizio with very little room to operate.

Once again, Cruz Rushing finds out how difficult Clarizio is to tackle. Clarizio jukes Rushing out of his socks in the backfield before reversing direction and cutting back across the formation against the original design of the play. He puts another defender in the blender, forcing Anthony Jones Jr. (No. 28) to miss a tackle and turning what should have been a negative play into a 10-yard gain.

This run reminded me a little of Kenneth Walker III. Sometimes the numbers aren’t in your favor, and you need a running back who can improvise and make a little magic happen on his own. Love to see it!

It was also nice to see some different faces on the field during this final possession, including redshirt freshman Braylon Collier (No. 17) at wide receiver, Antonio Johnson (No. 54) and Rustin Young (No. 73) along the offensive line, and true freshman Eddie Whiting (No. 84) at tight end. As forgettable as this game was, there was at least some value in getting these young guys game experience against a talented Oregon defense.

Final Thoughts: Just Beat butgers

Despite the lopsided loss to Oregon, I came away encouraged by what I saw from Kayd Coffman and Jace Clarizio.

That being said, Michigan State absolutely has to beat Rutgers this week. We’ve spent enough time talking about player development and building toward the future. I want Pat Fitzgerald to put the players on the field who give Michigan State the best chance to win, regardless of age or class. Send the seniors out with a victory and give Spartan fans something positive to take into the offseason.

I’m curious to hear from Spartan fans. Who would you like to see start at quarterback against Rutgers? Go back to Alessio Milivojevic if he’s healthy, give Cam Fancher one last shot, stick with Kayd Coffman or hand the reins over to Leo Hannan? Who gives Michigan State the best chance to win? Let me know in the comments.

Bottom line: Beat butgers. Whatever it takes. Kick 12 field goals. Win 2-0 because the Rutgers punter accidentally steps out of the back of the end zone. Run the ball 90 times and let the quarterback finish with more handoffs than a Chick-fil-A drive-thru. Fake a punt on 1st down. I don’t care.

Just win the damn game.

msu.body:
The NCAA Soccer Tournaments began this weekend with both the Michigan State Men’s and Women’s Teams hosting games.

The Spartans Women earned a #1 seed and faced 16th-seed Central Connecticut State on Saturday.  The game went the way a 1-vs.-16 game should go.  MSU won 7-0 to advance to the round of 32.  The Spartans had two goals each from Bella Najera, Kennedy Bell, and LJ Pearcy along with one from Lacey Kindel.  After leading 4-0 at the half, MSU got both their 2nd and 3rd string goalkeepers in after halftime.  None of the 3 goalies had to record a single save.

Here is the first Spartan goal, which proved to be the game winner.

Bella Najera scores her FOURTH goal of the postseason!  Sargeant and Briggs with the assists to give MSU a 1-0 lead. pic.twitter.com/xOTMEYdkRD
— Michigan State Women's Soccer (@MSU_wsoccer) November 21, 2026

MSU will host their round of 32 game as well.  That game will be this coming Friday, November 27, against Xavier.

The MSU Men also earned the right to play their first game at DeMartin Stadium as a 4-seed.  Unlike the women’s tournament with 64 teams, the men’s tourney only has 48 teams, so the top 4 seeds in each region get a bye to the round of 32.  MSU hosted Marshall today after the Thundering Herd took down Bowling Green on Thursday.

After 90 scoreless minutes, the game went to overtime.  There were no goals in the extra sessions either, so the game headed to penalty kicks.  Even as the higher seeded team and the home team, Marshall outperformed Michigan State for large portions of the game, winning the shots-on-goal battle, 8-5.  The Spartan goalie, Jake Grekowicz, made a couple of challenging saves in the overtimes that nearly ended the game.

In penalty kicks, Marshall was the first team up.  Both teams made their first two attempts.  In the third round, Marshall converted but MSU’s shot was saved.  Each team made their 4th attempt, so Marshall led 4-3 heading to the 5th with a chance to win with another successful PK.  Sadly, Grekowicz was unable to make a save and Marshall picked up the win.

Had MSU won, they would have hosted the round of 16 game as the 1-seed in the region, Akron, was knocked off by Wake Forest earlier in the day.  The season comes to an end for the Men’s Team.

The Lady Spartans move on.  Their 7-0 win was the second largest victory in the tournament’s opening round; Alabama beat Jackson State, 12-0!  Get ready to tune in to that game on Friday to root on the Green & White as they look to advance to the 3rd round.

msu.headline: El Niño hits Spartans in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks celebrates his teammates second half touchdown run against the Michigan State Spartans at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Lots going on in the world of MSU sports this weekend. So, we thought let’s have some weather report fun and incorporate basketball, hockey and football all into this week’s report. Football was an ugly blood bath that we all saw coming. Hockey pulls off a split but had its own blood bath brawl in Yost. Basketball saw some solid bench action but the post is not looking good with the center position. Fellow TOC writer O helped out with this report and the basketball sun and cloud are coming from him. Without further adieu let us step into some sunshine.

Sun #1

My first sun is for the Spartan football team and coaches. They lost 45-7 you say, how could you possibly award the team a sun? This team has looked bad, and have had some very ugly games. This team has also had injuries that have superceded the last two years and those years were bad. What has changed this year is character. The team has character and fight. They are giving their best and not giving up. The number of underclassmen getting playing time, the number of athletes that are not the four stars Oregon is sending out there are all getting strong character development in Spartan grit. Fitz has the team playing. I’d be interested to see if he can get better athletes and take a good look at conditioning and what is going on with all these injuries. I know there is one more game but next year will really be the year to see what Fitz can actually potentially do.

Sun #2

Sun two brings us to the ice. MSU hockey has been off to a tough start and has been disappointing. Struggling to find their chemistry and identity with all the youth and lacking a true leader. Well, this weekend against the weasels MSU had an opportunity to perhaps turn the season in the right direction. Friday was an ugly game where the Spartans were manhandled and it all started with an early power play that had MSU behind practically from the start. Then we get to the melee. The hip check that the weasels felt very offended by. Barnhill and Vansaghi may have fought life back into this team. Even with both players suspended for game two and into the OSU series, they maybe let out frustrations of an entire team in an early season. Saturday night, an entirely different MSU team took the ice. Down defenders, Ward and Jurecki brought energy and the sticks were active Saturday. MSU out shot, out played, and out scored the number one team in the country. They looked like the team we have been waiting for. Yes, the weasels were short forwards, but MSU was down defenders. Ravensbergen looked outstanding, except when he left his post open, but still had the shut out. This might be a breath of fresh air that they needed to get into the winning column. The team is talented, now let’s continue to play like it.

Sun #3

Our basketball sun is going to Kur Teng. Teng had a career high 24 points on 8/11, and 5/8 from 3. Teng showed he can be a reliable shooter for this team. This allows the team to not rely on Scott and Jervis and sometimes Fears for all the perimeter shooting. Teng has always been smooth from three but has never been consistent or had a break out performance. Hopefully Teng can get hot and be a weapon that draws coverage which can perhaps open up some paint play if the MSU big men can handle it.

Cloud #1

Football cloud goes to the teams health. MSU was doubled in yardage, had two turnovers, were terrible on third down and I’m still giving the cloud to health. The injuries on this team need to be figured out. Injuries have haunted this team for a few years now. So, what’s going on? Is there something going on in conditioning or practices? Is it dietary? Is it really just bad luck? Conditioning coaches have changed and we still have the problem. This year though, was unbearable. The injuries were so much it had to be difficult to game plan when you don’t end up having the players you need on the field. It is nearly impossible to be competitive against an Oregon with third string players and a freshman QB.

Cloud #2

As much as the brawl helped inspire my hockey sun, that same brawl inspires my hockey cloud. Losing Barnhill and Vansaghi for one game is bad enough. The reprucussions of suspensions could be greater and have implications down the road. Having a significant penalty means the two are going to have to stay out of trouble or a worse suspension will come their way. That is a tough ask for a player like Vansaghi who is the agitator  for MSU. He is the guy that comes to the defense of his teammates and will throw a punch at anyone. To have him have to change his way of play could be a learning process. In a team that needs a bit more leadership, Vansaghi is a guy that can provide that, the chip on the shoulder, and the aggression. MSU needs him, so the suspensions will be something to keep an eye on.

Cloud #3

Our basketball cloud has been hinted at some but we can officially say it now goes to the centers. Taylor, McCulloch and Bonke had three combined field goals. They had six turnovers. None of them can be relied upon to be fed the ball in the low post and make a move to beat a defender. They are only scoring on rebounded put backs or a wide open Fears feed. To make things worse, the coaching staff didn’t even try to run any of those sort of plays. Bonke has been disappointing all season and Taylor is still developing. Regardless, the Spartans need a lot more production from the big guys in the paint. MSU typically struggles at the arc but has had some success there this season. If they can get stronger in the block and stay hot outside, they will be very difficult to beat. Hopefully, they can work out these kinks before the schedule gets even tougher in B1G play.

There we have it. As a big follower and fan of MSU hockey, I was very happy to see this team look like itself and take down number 1 at Munn. That was my favorite moment of the weekend. The lineup changes may be the key to staying hot on the ice. As always, I look forward to seeing where your clouds and suns lie in the comments. I wish you all a Happy Thanksgiving and be thankful there’s only Rutgers left on the football schedule. Go Green!

tigers.headline: Tigers fortify their roster but managing it will be tricky in 2027
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers president of baseball operations Scott Harris (left) and manager A.J. Hinch (right) talk to reporters March 25, 2026, before Opening Day at Petco Park in San Diego, California. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

The addition of a quality veteran starting pitcher in the form of right-hander Kevin Gausman may be the final move in what has been a fast paced re-tooling effort this offseason. Detroit Tigers’ president of baseball operations Scott Harris has demphasized on shoring up weaknesses rather than pursuing a lot of top shelf talent. Nothing is going to replace the loss of Tarik Skubal, but by addressing the holes in the roster that sank them in 2026, the Tigers may be in a better position to weather the kind of storms that blew them well off course. The rest will depend on their young players improving.

Emilio Pagán is a quality high leverage relief addition, but not terribly exciting. He’s basically taking the space of Kenley Jansen as a, hopefully, more stable veteran closer. It doesn’t hurt that Pagán has already made clear that he’s not concerned with save chances and will pitch whenever they need him either. Luis Gil and Ha-Seong Kim are talented but come with huge question marks as the reclamation projects for the year. Harris, ever a Jed Hoyer disciple, loves a cheap bounceback candidate with injury and aging concerns. Someday one of them has to work out, right?

There wasn’t much to be excited about, but Kevin Gausman is bit bigger addition. Fortifying the starting rotation with a good pitcher with proven durability gives the Tigers a lot of options to convert their younger, less experienced starters into relievers, as least in 2027. The Gausman signing addresses the rotation and bullpen both. It hasn’t been a thrilling offseason and Harris remains very shy of making a big move that could turn into a big mistake, but some weak points in the roster have been fortified and they’ve built in more roster flexibility. They are still probably a big bat and another high leverage arm from really looking like a really legit contender in 2027, but if their young talent continues to develop they won’t need that much help.

The trick will be managing this roster optimally in 2027. Particularly the pitching staff. To actually bring their best 13 pitchers to bear on their major league opponents, rather than having struggling arms at the major league level that they can’t option while the Triple-A Toledo Mud Hens enjoy a stacked roster, they have to be quicker to jettison struggling veterans in favor of younger options. That type of scenario has been an issue for them in the past.

Here is the current complete 40-man roster with option status attached, plus RHP Luis Gil, SS Ha-Seong Kim, and RHP Kevin Gausman, all signed in the last few days to major league contracts. Three players still need to be DFA’d to make space for those three when their contracts become official following their physicals.

PitcherOptionsPosition PlayersOptionsRHP Drew AndersonNoDillon DinglerYesRHP Beau BrieskeNo Josue BriceñoYesLHP Enmanuel de JesusYesThayron LiranzoYesRHP Kyle FinneganNoMax AndersonYesRHP Brenan HanifeeYesJavier BáezNoLHP Tyler HoltonYesTsung-Tse ChengNoLHP Brant HurterYesPeyton GrahamYesRHP Jackson JobeYesColt KeithYesRHP Ty MaddenYesHao-Yu LeeYesRHP Troy MeltonYesKevin McGonigleYesRHP Keider MonteroYesJohn PeckYesRHP Reese OlsonYesSpencer TorkelsonYesRHP Emilio PagánNoBrett CallahanYesRHP RIver RyanYesKerry CarpenterYesLHP Andrew SearsYesMax ClarkYesLHP Drew SommersYesRiley GreeneYesLHP Framber ValdezNoBen MalgeriYesRHP Will VestNoZach McKinstryNoRHP Jacob WaguespackNoParker MeadowsYesRHP Luis GilNoWenceel PérezYesRHP Kevin GausmanNoEduardo ValenciaYesHa-Seong KimNo

For argument’s sake, let’s assume Tsung-Tse Cheng, Brenan Hanifee, and Beau Brieske will be the three designated for assignment to get down to 40 players. The Tigers have no money committed to those three, and at this point they’re pretty easily DFA’d.

Signing Ha-Seong Kim makes Cheng entirely expendable as he’s out of options, and the Tigers have John Peck and Peyton Graham on the roster to fill in at shortstop if McGonigle, Kim, and Báez aren’t enough. They even got Trey Sweeney back on a minor league deal after designating him.

You could posit a DFA of de Jesus instead of Brieske or Hanifee, perhaps, but de Jesus has options. Brieske doesn’t. There aren’t many other choices available without releasing a player on a major league deal like Waguespack, Finnegan, or Báez, where the Tigers would just eat their 2026 salary.

On the position player side, there’s no issue here. Javy Báez or Zach McKinstry may have to be DFA’d at some point to let younger players take those spots, but it’s up to the young players to push that duo off the roster. Meadows, Carpenter, and Pérez could use a bit of Triple-A time to get back in the groove after missing much of the 2026 season, but they all have options available. Younger players like John Peck, Ben Malgeri, and Brett Callahan are knocking at the major league door after debuts of varying success in 2026, but a little more seasoning at Triple-A won’t hurt them.

On the pitching side, things are trickier when you start composing a 13-man pitching staff.

Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman, and Troy Melton are your top three starters. The Tigers don’t have to start Melton, but we’ll take the long-term extension as a certain sign that they believe in him as a starter.

In the bullpen, you have Will Vest, Emilio Pagán, Drew Anderson, Jacob Waguespack, Luis Gil, and Kyle Finnegan, none of whom can be optioned. Gil and Anderson may compete for the final two rotation spots instead, but we’ll just pencil them in the bullpen for the moment. So, without releasing someone the 26-man roster has room for four more pitchers, two in the pen and two in the rotation. Let’s assume they’ll take at least two lefties in the bullpen, and we’ll go with Holton and Sommers. So now we have just the two rotation spots left available.

Again, just for argument’s sake, let’s bump Hanifee and Brieske off the roster for Gil and Gausman when their contracts are announced. To fill the two remaining spots in the rotation, here are your options.

Jackson Jobe

Keider Montero

River Ryan

Reese Olson

Brant Hurter

Ty Madden

Andrew Sears

Enmanuel de Jesus

Everyone in that group can be optioned, but you can only add two of them to the 26-man active roster at a time without jettisoning pitchers who don’t have options. You begin to see the potential difficulties here. Are the Tigers really going to put six of those eight pitchers in Triple-A while they try Finnegan, Waguespack, and Gil? How long will the Tigers take to adjust if players are guaranteed deals stuggle, and where is the depth remaining in the minors once moves like that are made?

There’s a fair chance that several talented pitchers will be in the minor leagues unless the Tigers are willing to eat some free agent contracts and pivot quickly if their veteran relievers struggle. And that’s really the rub here. Part of the reason that putting together a deep, homegrown group is such a good thing, as the Tigers have on the position player side, is that you have a lot of flexibility if someone struggles. That’s only helpful if you have useful prospects or Triple-A depth. The Tigers lack of pitching prospects right now creates a problem that they have to bridge in 2027 until a good crop of young pitchers nears the major leagues in 2028.

Managing all this will be a unique challenge, and we’ve seen the Tigers fail to cut bait in time on several occasions in the Harris era. With the additions of Gausman, Pagán, and Gil, the Tigers have built up a reasonably formidable and deep group of pitchers here. The trick is figuring out how to deploy this group to best effect. As we say every offseason, injuries make a lot of a team’s final roster decisions for them. It’s an extremely rare case when a team actually has “too much” pitching by the time the regular season actually gets underway, so this will presumably look less tricky to manage by the time Opening Day rolls around.

My current best guess at how this all shakes out on Opening Day is as follows, with Finnegan, Gil, and Waguespack on a short leash to start the year.

Rotation- Valdez, Gausman, Melton, Montero, Jobe

Bullpen- Vest, Pagán, Gil, Waguespack, Anderson, Sommers, Holton, Finnegan

That leaves two of the Tigers most talented pitchers, River Ryan and Reese Olson, starting the year in the minor leagues along with a talented left-hander in Brant Hurter, with all three coming off injured seasons. That’s not ideal, and so we’re already faced with releasing two of Finnegan, Waguespack, and Gil before the season even starts. It’s easy enough to release any of those three, but now the depth we’re talking about is used up, and they don’t really have a lot of relief options to backfill into the 40-man roster at Toledo. Again, spring injuries will sort some of this out, but they’ll face tough choices if those pitchers without options are struggling.

The Tigers should at least have pretty good southpaw depth for the bullpen in Triple-A with Hurter, Enmanuel de Jesus, and Andrew Sears. They also signed LHP Jake Miller, a talented but injury plagued prospect, to a minor league deal after designating him last week.

All in all, that’s a deep pitching staff to work with, even if no one can actually replace Tarik Skubal’s impact in leading the rotation. But there is plenty of uncertainty to go with the potential, and the flexibility just isn’t very good. The Tigers were undone by their supporting cast in 2025-2026, and without any long-term commitments, Harris has managed to build in more options. It’s just another group of risky, older players who could rapidly become anchors on the Tigers’ performance if they struggle and management doesn’t pivot fast enough.

We’d love another impact bat and a reliever like Bryan Abreu to really tie the whole thing together, but there isn’t much available in free agency, and the signing of Kim probably says Harris is done with the infield. We can dream of a trade, but in four years we’ve yet to see Harris swap prospects for good major league talent.

Management of this roster by Harris and AJ Hinch is going to be crucial. They have plenty of talent but fewer sure things than the top tier teams around the league. It’s also a somewhat ill-fitting group in terms of contracts and option status. Gausman and Pagán are nice additions, and Kim and Gil are nice fliers to take. How much production they can squeeze from this tangled but talented supporting cast may be the difference between a memorable season and another dud.

tigers.headline: Tigers to sign RHP Kevin Gausman to one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 23: Kevin Gausman #12 of the Chicago Cubs celebrates during the fifth inning against the Miami Marlins at Wrigley Field on September 23, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Scott Harris and Jeff Greenberg continue to pile up major league free agent signings. On Wednesday evening, Jeff Passan of ESPN reported that the Detroit Tigers are in agreement with veteran right-handed starting pitcher Kevin Gausman on a one-year deal worth $25 million. The deal is pending a physical.

The 35-year-old Gausman has been one of the more durable and effective starters in baseball over the last decade. He’s topped 170 innings in each of the last six seasons, pitching in 2020-2021 for the San Francisco Giants, where Scott Harris was the GM at the time, and then the Toronto Blue Jays from 2022-2026. The Jays traded him to the Chicago Cubs at the 2026 trade deadline, where he finished the season.

Gausman will mix in his slider occasionally, but he’s essentially a two-pitch pitcher, utilizing his fourseam fastball and outstanding splitter almost exclusively. He used the fourseamer 50.6 percent of the time in 2026, averaging 93.8 mph with above average extension. It’s not quite the bat misser it was when Gausman threw a little harder, but his command and good life on the pitch have continued to make it an effective fastball. His splitter continues to rack up a huge amount of swing and miss, with hitters whiffing 42.9 percent of the time in 2026.

Gausman struck out 24.5 percent of hitters faced last season, with his customary low walk rate of 6.3 percent. He’s typically suppressed home runs quite well, especially in the last half decade, but he did finally have a couple of rough outings with the Cubs in which he gave up more homers than usual. Transitioning to a new team with new catchers, in a ballpark that can be favorable to the long ball in the summertime, probably explains all of it. Gausman is still an above average starting pitcher, and we’re not going to put too much into his rough two months in Chicago. However, his 4.51 ERA was his worst, and the first time he’s been over 4.00, since 2019.

Adding Gausman is probably an upgrade to the Tigers’ starting rotation. Framber Valdez, Gausman, and after signing a long-term deal, Troy Melton can all be inked into the Opening Day rotation. That would leave Jackson Jobe, Keider Montero, Luis Gil, River Ryan, Drew Anderson, Reese Olson, and Andrew Sears theoretically vying for the final two spots in the rotation. That’s quite a lot of pitching depth, and assuming the injuries are at a normal level next year, should allow them to flex a few of those pitchers into the bullpen.

Where this is hard to process, is in the fact that by building in all this depth with major league signings, the Tigers risk pushing some optionable pitchers off the 40-man roster. If everything works out, they’ll have so much pitching it shouldn’t matter, but if some of these pitchers don’t perform as hoped, and there are always at least a few, they’re going to clog up the 26-man roster to a degree. That’s probably a risk worth taking, because pitchers like River Ryan and Olson, if he’s finally healthy, aren’t built up to throw a starter’s workload anyway, but the roster crunch is going to be real if spring camp concludes with most of these pitchers healthy. Of course, at that point teams are desperate for pitching, and the Tigers might even have an opportunity to trade from a deeply stacked hand.

Gausman’s 2026 numbers lend themselves to a little concern that he may be tipping into a real decline phase, but his stuff, his strikeout and walk rates, and his contact data all look normal. He certainly adds veteran presence and a long, long track record of consistent good performance to the Tigers’ starting rotation. It feels like overkill to a degree, with the Tigers still not exactly stocked with high leverage relief options even after adding Emilio Pagán, but the uncertain medical status of players like Olson and Will Vest has to be factored into the equation as well. They’ve been rumored to have interest in RHP Bryan Abreu, the top right-handed reliever left in free agency, but my guess would be this puts an end to that speculation.

The Tigers will need to DFA two pitchers to open spots for Gil and Gausman, as well as a position player to make room for Ha-Seong Kim. There are only so many major league pitching signings you can make before you’re pushing useful, and just as importantly, optionable pitchers off the 40-man roster. Still, as long as the additions are upgrades, it’s hard to go wrong. If the Tigers manage their staff well and move the right starting pitchers to the bullpen, they should be pretty strong in both the rotation and the bullpen.

tigers.headline: Get to know your Tigers Rookies of the Year
tigers.body:
Tigers great Lou Whitaker was introduced during a ceremony to retire Whitaker's No. 1 before the game against the Rays on Saturday, Aug. 6, 2022, at Comerica Park. Tigers2 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

We were all thrilled around here when the 2026 American League Rookie of the Year award went to Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle. He was certainly a worthy candidate: he led the American League in WAR (according to Baseball Reference), which is mighty impressive. But did you know he also led the league in plate appearances? Nobody in the league came to the plate more often than McGonigle, which shows you just how reliable and durable he was as a centerpiece of the Tigers’ lineup.

Five other Detroit Tigers have won the Rookie of the Year award, which began in 1947; for the first two years there was only one awarded across Major League Baseball, with individual leagues giving out their awards in 1949. That doesn’t seem like too many, and perhaps it isn’t, but I think you’ll agree some of the Tigers who have won these awards have been pretty special players. (All WAR values are bWAR, because I love Baseball Reference

#1: Harvey Kuenn (1953)

Rookie WAR: 1.7

Career WAR: 25.8 (15 seasons)

Career batting average/OPS/OPS+: .303/.765/108

Kuenn (pronounced “keen”) was from Wisconsin, attended the University of Wisconsin, and later went on to manage the Milwaukee Brewers to their only previous American League pennant (although they fell to the Cardinals in the 1982 World Series). But he made his mark in Michigan on some pretty terrible Tigers teams of the 1950s, after foregoing his final year of college eligibility in 1952 to briefly play in the Tigers’ minor-league system before permanently becoming a major-leaguer in September of that year.

Like McGonigle, Kuenn led the American League in plate appearances. He also led the league in hits, and in 731 plate appearances he struck out a scant 31 times. He would never strike out 40 times in a season, which is totally bonkers by today’s standards. Kuenn easily beat Boston’s Tom Umphlett for the Rookie of the Year award; Umphlett would have two more forgettable years in Washington and then spend another decade in the minor leagues.

While Kuenn didn’t hit many home runs — his career-high was a dozen in 1956 — he could certainly hit line drives for doubles, leading the American League in two-baggers three times. In 1958 he moved to the outfield and would occasionally play third base as well. He was also involved in one of the most famous trades in baseball history: just before the 1960 season, after leading the American League with a .353 batting average in 1959, he was traded to Cleveland for Rocky Colavito, who’d led the league in home runs with 49 in ‘59. Can you imagine that trade?! Holy moly.

After a year in Cleveland he spent several seasons with the Giants, Cubs and Phillies, mostly playing in the outfield but transitioning to primarily pinch-hitting by the end of his career in 1966. He was the Brewers’ hitting coach for most of the 1970s, and became their manager for two seasons in the early 1980s. He was plagued by heart and circulation issues, and had part of a leg amputated before he turned 50, dying of a heart attack before 60.

#2: Mark Fidrych (1976)

Rookie WAR: 9.6

Career WAR: 11.4 (5 seasons)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.10/126

What can you say about Fidrych that hasn’t already been said? He was, at the same time, both larger than life and completely down to Earth. His flame burned white-hot for one season, and then an injury took him down immediately after and he never recovered. What could he have done in a full career? Would he have been one of the all-time greats, or another Joe Charboneau? Nobody knows.

In the Appalachian League in 1974, the lanky Fidrych had quite the head of curly hair; his manager thought he looked a bit like a bird, and the nickname stuck. In 1976 he started the season in the bullpen, being used sparingly before moving into the rotation. He completed 24 (!!) of his 29 starts, throwing four shutouts along the way. The famous “Yankees Game” saw him go the distance on national television; if you have never watched that game, my goodness, take the next two-plus hours and do just that. It is incredible and delightful and amazing for a boatload of reasons.

(Did you know Rusty Staub was afraid of flying, and was a gourmet cook? The announcers mentioned that seconds before a fly ball caught the right-field overhang at Tiger Stadium.)

If you don’t have two-plus hours to spare, skip to the ninth inning in the video. The Stadium is going nuts, Fidrych is clearly way too hyped-up but he closes it out with a grounder to second, and after the final out he shakes the hands of his teammates, umpires, the grounds crew, fans, and probably a police officer. He’s barely old enough to legally order a beer, and almost fifty thousand people chanted his name to get him out on the field to tip his cap. You can watch a lot of baseball games and never see anything quite like that.

Did the massive workload take a toll on Fidrych’s body? Probably, but in the ‘70s it wasn’t unheard-of for a pitcher to finish more than half of his starts. (Mind you, plenty of pitchers suffered career-ending injuries because of it; the Nolan Ryans and Mickey Loliches of the world were the exceptions.) He hurt his knee in spring training the following year, but came back in May and was as dominant as he’d been the year before. But in July he felt something go wrong in his arm, and tried to pitch through it but he was never the same. As it turns out, he tore his rotator cuff — a serious but hardly career-ending ailment these days — and his career ended in 1980.

Fidrych went back to his native Massachusetts and lived a quiet life: he drove a truck and bought a farm, marrying and having a daughter. Sadly, like Kuenn before him, he would die much too young: in 2009 he was working underneath a truck, which fell and killed him. (I was at a Tigers game that day with my brother, and we heard the news during dinner at Gar’s Bar in Marine City, Michigan. I don’t believe I was able to finish my Garburger.)

#3: Lou Whitaker (1978)

Rookie WAR: 3.8

Career WAR: 75.1 (19 seasons)

Career batting average/OPS/OPS+: .286/.789/117

As long as Whitaker is not in the Baseball Hall of Fame, I will not set one foot in Cooperstown, New York.

Drafted out of high school in Virginia, he started off as a third baseman in the minor leagues, but switched to second base in 1977 while playing at Double-A Montgomery alongside a shortstop you may know. Famously, both he and the shortstop were called up to the Tigers on the same day, making their major-league debuts in the second game of a doubleheader at Fenway Park on Friday, September 9, 1977.

Neither he nor the shortstop hit too many home runs in 1978: Whitaker had three of the total five between the pair. But both of them would find power within a few years, Whitaker topping twenty home runs four times in an era in which that was an unusual feat for a middle infielder. Early in his career, defence was Whitaker’s calling card, and in his rookie year that was undeniably true: his Range Factor per 9 innings was tops in the American League, and it would be above the league average every year for the first five years of his career.

If you were a Tiger fan in the 1980s, it was easy to take Whitaker and the shortstop for granted. They were just there, day after day, being extremely good baseball players. Getting on base, hitting some home runs, and turning more double plays than any other pair of teammates in history. I doubt that record will ever be broken: can you imagine two teammates playing side-by-side for nineteen straight seasons, almost every day, at two crucial defensive positions?

The question about Whitaker has always been, was he merely “good” and not “great” as one might expect from a Hall of Famer? I know WAR is a counting statistic (and there are things you can say about such things), but the fact that the only six second basemen above him in career WAR are in the Hall of Fame — and another fourteen below him in career WAR are in there as well — needs to count for something. You need to be durable, consistent, and more than anything else, very very good at what you do, to put up cumulative numbers like that.

I’m biased, of course: I want Whitaker to be in the Hall of Fame, right beside the shortstop. It would’ve been great if they’d been inducted at the same time, but that did not happen. The shortstop went on at length about how Whitaker belonged there in his acceptance speech, as he should have. Your move, Cooperstown.

#4: Justin Verlander (2006)

Rookie WAR: 4.0

Career WAR: 82.3 (21 seasons)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.33/128

For those of you who have been living under either a rock or some other heavy object for the past couple of decades, Verlander was a pitcher who was very good for a very long time who retired after the 2026 season, rejoining the Tigers for one last go-round after being with them from 2005 to the midpoint of the 2017 season.

Verlander was drafted in 2004, the second pick overall out of Old Dominion University in Virginia. (Matt Bush was first overall that year; he took a circuitous route to the Major Leagues, to put it bluntly.) He started the 2005 season in High-A Lakeland, mowing down hitters with ruthless efficiency before being promoted to Double-A Erie where he did the same thing. He made two starts with Detroit that season, but those didn’t go so well. Thankfully that wouldn’t be the case the following year when he came north with the Tigers out of Spring Training and didn’t look back.

The 2006 season was pure magic for Tigers fans, and Verlander’s role on that team was a significant one. He made 30 starts, went 17-9, and easily won the Rookie of the Year award over second-place finisher Jonathan Papelbon. (Four other people receiving votes in either league ended up playing for the Tigers at some point: Francisco Liriano, Ian Kinsler, Anibal Sánchez and Prince Fielder. Neat)

You probably know the rest of his story: three Cy Young awards, a league MVP, some no-hitters, the deadline trade to Houston and the subsequent World Series rings which stung more than a little. (He also finished second in the Cy Young voting three times.) He’s as much of a lock to go into the Hall of Fame on the first ballot; the only question in my mind is, will he be the second-ever unanimous pick, or will Miguel Cabrera beat him to that? His 266 career wins might just be the highest total we see in a pitcher from here on out.

The Tigers signed him to pitch for the 2026 season, and he was injured in his first start of the year in Arizona after three innings. He worked hard all season, despite some setbacks, to pitch one last time — which he did on the season’s penultimate day, against the Pirates. He acquitted himself well, pitching into the sixth and only allowing two runs on the day. Weird fact: the only two times he pitched that season were against National League teams. I still hate interleague play (but I loved watching American League pitchers bat).

#5: Michael Fulmer (2016)

Rookie WAR: 5.4

Career WAR: 12.8 (9 seasons so far)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.93/110

This one is still a work in progress, as Fulmer is still pitching — when he can stay healthy, that is.

Originally drafted by the New York Mets, he came to the Tigers as a minor-leaguer in the trade that sent the mercurial Yoenis Céspedes away. Like Fidrych, Fulmer has been through injury troubles for most of his major-league career; unlike Fidrych, there are now surgeries and techniques that could have easily fixed Fidrych’s problems.

His rookie season in Detroit came at a strange time for the franchise; the core group of players that saw so much success in the first half of the decade was starting to fray and age, but could Fulmer lead a youthful resurgence to return the team to the top of the league again? (No, as it turns out.) He did well, though: an 11-7 record in 26 starts, keeping the ball in the yard for the most part. Like others of his generation, he didn’t really start finding his strikeout groove until a couple of years in the Majors, but he generally kept the Tigers in the game.

Alas, the all-too-common Tommy John surgery was performed in 2019 after feeling something in a Spring Training game, and he missed all of that season before some short, unsuccessful starts in the abbreviated 2020 campaign. He saw quite a bit of success in the bullpen in 2021 and 2022; at the trade deadline in 2022 he was dealt to the Twins in exchange for Sawyer Gipson-Long. He spent 2023 with the Cubs before needing more elbow surgery, taking him out for the following season.

In 2025 he pitched once for the Red Sox before rejoining the Cubs, and he split the 2026 season between the Angels and the Yankees. I’d say he’s now successfully reached “journeyman” status, but you have to wonder how long his arm can hold up before it breaks again. Who knows? He might pitch into his late 40s, doing a pretty credible Jamie Moyer impersonation.

How will we summarize McGonigle’s career when it’s all over? It’s impossible to predict, but by all meaningful measures he seems to be set up for long-term success so long as he stays healthy. I hope we can look back on his career and say phrases like “realized potential” and “sure-thing Hall of Famer;” time will tell, though.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign SS Ha-Seong Kim to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 07: Atlanta shortstop Ha-Seong Kim (7) takes batting practice prior to the start of the NLDS game 4 between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Atlanta Braves on October 7th, 2026 at Truist Park in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

At Troy Melton’s extension press conference on Tuesday morning, Scott Harris hinted that a move to shore up their infield defense was already in the works. It didn’t take long, as Jeff Passan of ESPN reports that the Tigers are in agreement with free agent shortstop Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year deal worth $5 million. Mark Feinsand of MLB.com reports that the deal includes another million dollars in performance bonuses that can be earned.

The Tigers have been linked to the 31-year-old infielder in previous offseasons, but nothing ever emerged. Kim has dealt with a litany of injuries in recent years, leaving the memory of his strong 2023-2024 campaigns with the San Diego Padres a bit distant. Kim had labrum issues with attendant inflammation in his right shoulder, his throwing arm, in late 2024 and 2025 that really limited him. He had surgery on the shoulder after the 2024 season and missed much of the 2025 season recovering.

He signed a one-year deal with the Braves last offseason, but a tendon injury to his right middle finger after a slip and fall on ice in his native South Korea required surgery and sent him repeatedly back to the injured list through the year. He appeared in just 51 games and couldn’t swing the bat at all, hitting just .116 on the year. The injury also affected his throwing and it was just a disaster of a season all around.

Scott Harris loves a cheap bet on a player to rebound from injury, and this is another example. Those bets have been failures. The recent signing of right-hander Luis Gil is another example of a deal where the risk is low and the reward fairly high, but the odds are pretty poor of it working out as hoped. Cumulatively, they’ve flushed a lot of money down the drain this way with nothing to show for it while avoiding obvious upgrades that would’ve required a more significant investment.

Kim was a star for the Kiwoom Heroes in the KBO for a few years before coming stateside. He signed a four-year deal worth $28 million with the San Diego Padres during the 2020-2021 offseason. He started off slowly in 2021, but from 2022-2024 was a consistent 3-4 WAR sort of player with excellent defense and roughly league average production at the plate.

After so much trouble with his shoulder, it’s not at all clear the Tigers will even get the defensive portion of Kim’s former abilities here. The finger injury at least seems like something that a long period of rest would have resolved. Labrum issues in your throwing arm are a lot more serious, though at least there was no reported trouble with the shoulder during his attempts to get back into form last year.

This is a small enough deal to just dump if John Peck cleans up his defense a little more and looks more capable of playing an above average shortstop. The problem is actually being willing to cut your losses quickly, which is something Harris has struggled with. There’s at least the chance that with all this time off, Kim will finally be well beyond the shoulder problems and ready to start getting back to his old form.

It’s a small bet on that possibility, but one would hate to see Peck have a strong spring camp only to get sidelined again while the Tigers run another low cost experiment. It’s also odd to make a move like this and not insist on a club option for 2028 in case it works out. Hard to believe many teams were clamoring for a player who arguably should be getting a minor league deal with an invite to spring camp Essentially, this is just a depth move, and so how they handle that competition for playing time, and how long they stick with Kim if he can’t get it going at the plate, is the crux of the issue.

tigers.headline: Teruaki Sato signs with Cubs, Freddy Peralta heads to Baltimore, and the Troy Melton extension is official
tigers.body:
TORONTO, ON - SEPTEMBER 14: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers pitches during a game against the Toronto Blue Jays at Rogers Centre on September 14, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. (Photo by Vaughn Ridley/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the biggest of all free agents this offseason signed as Tarik Skubal agreed to a monster deal worth $450 million, the other big names are starting to come off the board in a hurry with a week left until owners lock out the players.

On Tuesday morning. longtime Hanshin Tigers star utilityman and slugger Teruaki Sato reportedly agreed to a six-year deal worth $120 million. The 2025 Nippon Professional Baseball MVP, who won the Triple Crown in 2026, joins an already potent Cubs positional group.

Not long after that deal dropped, right-hander Freddy Peralta was reported to have agree with the Baltimore Orioles on a five-year deal totaling $125 million. The former Milwaukee Brewers starter was traded to the New York Mets last offseason before his final year of team control. It went quite poorly, but after Peralta was traded to the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade deadline he was able to turn things around somewhat. While never an ace, the 30-year-old was a generally durable frontline starter for the Brewers. Even so, that’s a pretty big contract for a pitcher whose current projections look decidedly more like a fairly average mid-rotation arm.

The Cleveland Guardians also got into the mix a bit, signing longtime Royals left-hander Kris Bubic to a one-year contract worth $17.5 million. He’s been a good but oft-injured starting pitcher in Kansas City for most of his career. Since his 2023 Tommy John surgery, he’s had myriad rotator cuff and forearm issues that continue to limit his workload. Joining Cleveland’s vaunted pitching program will likely make him a bigger problem for the AL Central, but only if he finally puts the injuries behind him. That seems unlikely, but it’s a solid low risk speculative signing of the sort the Guardians prefer.

On Tuesday, the Tigers officially announced Troy Melton’s six-year extension which guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives, bonuses, and a club option that could make it a seven-year deal worth $80 million in total.

The Tigers officially announcing the Melton extension. pic.twitter.com/2YGpbMX828
— Rogelio C (@therogcast) November 24, 2026

There are still some big names out there in free agency. Top reliever Adrian Morejon, and outfielders Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are still available. As Sato plays some right field as well as third base, it will be interesting to see if the Cubs circle back to Suzuki at this point, but it seems much more likely that they’re out of the market for the 32-year-old.

Overall, free agency is moving very quickly and just about all the big names seem set on getting deals done before the lockout. Whether that signals a belief in the owners getting a salary cap in place, or whether Skubal’s massive contract and the flurry of signings means that players are trying to avoid the waiting game and uncertainly of a potentially long lockout is still anyone’s guess. With the Tigers still in need of some upgrades in the bullpen and perhaps the infield, we’ll see if Scott Harris has anything else to come, or whether at this point they think it better to let the CBA play out and see if the new payroll structure in the next CBA creates some opportunities.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign right-hander Luis Gil to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
Apr 26, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Luis Gil (81) delivers a pitch during the second inning against the Houston Astros at Daikin Park. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Tigers made another minor move on Sunday to shore up their pitching depth. Jeff Passan reports that the Tigers have signed RHP Luis Gil to a one-year deal worth $2.3 million, with a potential two million more in incentives. The deal is still pending a physical. Gil was non-tendered by the New York Yankees on Friday after a rough season on the mound for the 28-year-old veteran.

Gil’s career has already been a pretty wild ride despite his relative youth. The six-foot-three, 215 pound right-hander was initially signed as an international free agent out of the Dominican Republic as a teenager by the Minnesota Twins. In 2018, the Twins dealt him to the Yankees for outfielder Jake Cave. Gil developed into an excellent prospect in the Yankees’ system with eye-popping strikeout numbers, and eventually made his major league debut in 2021. The next season he blew out his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. He returned in 2024 and put together a strong campaign that earned him the AL Rookie of the Year award. A lat strain in 2025 and back issues in 2026 have limited him in the interim to just 84.1 innings over the last two seasons.

There are some reasons for optimism. Gil still has good velocity, sitting 95.3 mph on his fourseamer in 2026, though that’s down over a full mile per hour from his peak a few years back. He has good riding action on the pitch at the top of the zone, along with plus extension. His slider and changeup are both quality plus pitches. At his best he’s electric. He just hasn’t been able to stay on the mound long enough to get in a groove the past two years. His command has never been particularly good, and his walk rates have spiked as the injuries took their toll, but he’ll throw enough strikes to make it work if healthy.

We’ll be curious to hear what Tigers’ president of baseball operations, Scott Harris, has to say about this acquisition. There’s a very good argument that Gil would be better off as a reliever. He topped out at 98.4 mph in 2026, despite the ongoing back troubles. If he can sit 97-98 mph in short bursts he’d be pretty electric with a plus slider-changeup combination. At the same time, he can come to camp as starting depth if needed as well.

Hopefully the medicals come back clean. The Tigers have not had much success keeping their pitchers healthy at any level of the organization. That’s a leaguewide problem, but the Tigers have had it worse than many if we put the whole farm system into the equation. The club has already made changes this offseason, hiring Scott Peters as their new medical director and Jeremiah Randall as head athletic trainer and physical therapist, so there’s clearly an emphasis on trying to address the problem.

Ultimately, this is a small, low risk move of the sort Harris favors. Yet Gil has a lot of talent if his body will just cooperate and the club could come out way ahead with this signing if they can get him right.
